#3784. Ahead of GTA 6 and as concerns over genAI PC ports grow, Take-Two's CEO says they're revving up their "technical defences" and "legal activites" over piracy

"[Piracy is] going to become more of a challenge… and we're aware of that"

It's a bit of a time for AI and games at the moment, 'ey? A bad time, obviously, as it's infecting everything from game development, to the modding community, to native PC ports of a remake of a very popular game that I won't link to for fear of a certain company finding out where I live and ending me there and then. And of course, the latter may be a concern for one Rockstar Games and the impending release of GTA 6. But according to Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick, game's publisher, they are currently technically and legally preparing themselves.

IGN recently spoke to Zelnick regarding potential AI cloning concerns, notably about any business issues they may face as a result. "I don't think it’s a financial matter, in terms of a threat to our business," Zelnick explained. "I do think it’s a creative matter. It's important to everyone, our developers and our consumers alike, to deliver the experience Rockstar envisions. And at the same time, of course, we protect our intellectual property vigilantly. So we are focused on these concerns. We're not in the least cavalier about them. Technology is advancing quickly. And at the same time, I do think that pretty much everyone wants the Rockstar experience as Rockstar intended."

Zelnick also made a comment about thinking "all companies should be protecting intellectual property, their own and everyone else's," in response to a question about whether he wants to see OpenAI follow in Claude's footsteps by limiting the potential for genAI clones. "If you're in the intellectual property business, which Anthropic is and OpenAI is, then it seems ironic on the one hand to stomp on someone else's IP and hope that yours is protected," he said.

It was during an investor Q&A where Zelnick dug into the precautions Take-Two are take-twoing in regards to the growing threat of AI. "[Piracy is] going to become more of a challenge… and we're aware of that. So we are utterly focused on enhancing our technical defenses and enhancing our legal activities appropriately. And at the same time, without in any way being cavalier, every entertainment business that exists is subject to some element of piracy. So this is likely to invade our business to a greater or lesser extent. I think it will be manageable and we are focused on it."

Essentially: unless you want to face the wrath of the kinds of lawyers multi-billion dollar companies can afford, I wouldn't bother trying to clone GTA 6 with AI! Probably won't end well!

PlayStation's once ambitious plans for PC seem to have softened considerably in recent months with reports suggesting Sony is moving away from porting first-party games to PC as it has done with The Last of Us, Uncharted, God of War, and more. In another shift toward console exclusivity, Sony Interactive Entertainment is now pulling the PlayStation Plus app from PC due to a low user rate. The app will no longer be available to PlayStation Plus users on PC starting December 10.

"PlayStation believes in providing high-quality experiences to our players, and we regularly review offerings to ensure we are focusing on experiences our members value most," SIE senior director of content acquisitions and operations Adam Michel says at the bottom of a PlayStation Blog announcing the latest PS Plus additions. Michel says "a very small number of eligible PlayStation Plus Premium members (less than 0.4%)" are using the PC app. "Making this change allows us to focus on enhancing high-quality experiences that more of our members want to use."

Back in May, Bloomberg reported that PlayStation's studio business group CEO Hermen Hulst had informed staff that Sony's big-budget story-driven games would no longer come to PC and instead be PlayStation console exclusives going forward. And in September, former SIE worldwide studios president Shuhei Yoshida suggested Sony could be reverting to its "older ways" of focusing on the "platform business" instead of trying to get its first-party games into as many hands as possible.

Sony itself has yet to publicly acknowledge its apparent trend away from the PC side of its games business, but just looking at how much PC ports of PlayStation games have slowed down in recent months and years, it does seem clear there's been something of a shift in focus. What that means for the next generation of PlayStation games and consoles is unclear, but another one of the company's former leaders thinks "true innovation" means a $300 PS6.

Why is PC gaming outpacing consoles? "PC players have a bit more choice," analyst says, and PC has "really strong momentum" as PlayStation and Xbox struggle

In a new episode of Nightdive's Deep Dive podcast releasing later today, legendary voice actor Stephen Russell spoke about his experience portraying the protagonist of the Thief series, Garrett. We also got final confirmation of something Nightdive had been teasing for awhile: Russell will be reprising the role in the new Tarnished Mirror expansion coming with the Thief remaster on December 3.

I don't think I realized before this interview that Thief was Russell's very first videogame role. Before working with Looking Glass, he had experience in theater, radio and "medical reads" where he had to pronounce complex disease names in an even, doctorly cadence.

Russell said that he felt able to let loose for the first time as Garrett, channeling Clint Eastwood to nail the rogue's singular noirish rasp. Russell hadn't been much into games, with his main frame of reference being simple arcade and educational fare, so he was struck when he first saw an early build of Thief, still remembering "the incredible claustrophobia they had created."

Recalling the creative ferment of Looking Glass in the '90s, Russell said that he had "never seen so many sleep-deprived people in [his] life." He also affectionately recalled the studio's habit of pulling devs out of their office chairs to fill out games' VO roles alongside the professionals: "Having got my start as an actor in community theater, it felt very familiar," Russell quipped. "You're not painting the sets today, today you're playing the lead role!"

Even after a long career appearing in the likes of Fallout, The Elder Scrolls, and Dishonored, Russell still counts Garrett as one of his favorite roles, and said that playing both the protagonist (Garrett) and antagonist (Father Karras) in Thief 2⁠—and having so few people realize he was voicing Karras⁠—remains one of his proudest acting achievements.

And Russell seems chuffed to be returning to the role of Garrett so many years later. "The writing this time around is just as strong as the first time and honors what was created originally," Russell said, adding that it was "great to be back with the old guy."

It's honestly just lovely to see how much this role still means to Russell, and that he's as happy to be returning as Garrett as we will be to hear him. Tarnished Mirror is shaping up to be a real "our powers combined" sort of project, as development was headed up by the team behind the beloved Thief: The Black Parade mod from 2023. You'll be able to listen to the full interview on Nightdive's YouTube channel later today, and you can wishlist Thief Remastered on Steam.

#3780. Sony have cancelled Fairgame$, once again reminding us that chasing live service big bucks basically never works

You know, I'm sure that Sony had every intention of following through on their intention to release 10 live service games by 2026, as they mentioned way back in 2022. Well, as far as an intention that's designed to please shareholders can go, anyway. And now here we are, almost five years on from that comment that continues to haunt them with the news Fairgame$ has been cancelled.

This comes from a report from Bloomberg, who shared that, thankfully, there are no planned job cuts due to the game being cancelled. In a statement, Sony said that, "The studio will shift its focus to collaborating with other development teams across PlayStation Studios, while also exploring new creative opportunities, though didn't go into detail as to who those other teams are.

Bloomberg were also privy to a note shared with developers at Haven Studios from executives Sean Decker and John Doyle that follows a recent test of the game: "While the test demonstrated strong operational excellence, live ops readiness and community engagement, player feedback and retention results were mixed and fell short of the goals we had set. Combined with challenging market conditions in the PVP shooter genre, we have made the difficult decision to cease development on the game."

Sony have, notably, failed to capitalise on the live service trend; I'm sure I don't need to remind you about Concord. Hell, this isn't even taking the end of Destiny 2 into consideration, once a driving force of live service games, or how Marathon has struggled to pick up an audience in the way that Sony may want it to. You just can't force a game to be popular, especially in a genre like shooters.

For those that either missed or forgot about Fairgame$, it was announced back in 2023 and was supposed to be a "competitive modern heist game where you team up to break into exotic locations and steal the cargo," all while taking on security and other, real people. Gameplay was never formally revealed, only a CGI trailer, and was set to come to PC as well as PlayStation. Bloomberg also noted that the game had been reworked multiple times since the announcement and was set to be re-revealed with a new name. Ultimately, it looks like Katharine was a little generous with her timeline of six months.

The Outer Worlds 2 is finally getting its DLC. Obsidian has announced that Side Effects Guaranteed, the first of a "two-part expansion" series, will launch on December 2. The devs had been promising DLC since before launch as part of the RPG's $100 Premium Edition, but you'd be forgiven for worrying that those promises were forgotten amid the massive shakeup at the studio.

The first part of Side Effects Guaranteed will offer a new region to explore on Eden, a boosted level cap with new perks grab, four new flaws to spice up your build, new gear, and an additional radio station. The story will have you working with one of two Sub Rosa agents as you decide what to do with the hibernating crew of a derelict ship.

We spoke with Obsidian about The Outer Worlds 2 DLC shortly after the game's launch last year, and at that time they'd only begun to sketch out plans for the expansion. But at least one thing has carried over from those high-level ideas: "Maybe we'll lean a bit harder into some of the more minor factions, like Sub Rosa, and build them out a little bit," game director Brandon Adler told us in 2025, and that part of the plan seems to have borne out.

But a lot has happened at Obsidian since we had that chat. It's now under Bethesda's direct management and working on a new Fallout game as part of Xbox's big shakeup. Obsidian was not immune to the mass layoffs at the publisher, and seemingly had an Avowed sequel stripped away as Xbox pointed it to return to the more lucrative Fallout franchise.

While The Outer Worlds 2 was one of our favorite games of 2025, it never appeared to make much of a splash among the broader gaming community. Its fans feared that slow sales might lead to the DLC being canceled, and there's still some fear that the expansions have been truncated so Obsidian can move onto Fallout more quickly.

#3778. Sick BMX flips, colourful characters, a whole lot of mail and a charming raccoon dog await you in Tanuki: Pon's Summer, which you can pick up now

Right, today's been miserable thanks to the now hourly discourse we have to all take part in lest we be seen as approving of the current bad thing, how about something that looks simply pleasant? Today's the launch day for Tanuki: Pon's Summer, a delightfully vibrant mail delivery sim/Tony Hawk's Pro Skater but for bikes about restoring a shrine before the end of summer.

I've been enamoured by the vibe of Tanuki: Pon's Summer since it was announced in no small part because of how in some small ways it reminds me of Boku No Natsuyasumi, a cult-classic, Japan-only game series that's mostly just about hanging out in the Japanese countryside. This one isn't so lackadaisical, as you do have a job to do in delivering mail, but I think a similar spirit is there.

When it comes to delivering mail, there is a Death Strandingian element to it in your need to place your boxes on your BMX (which you can do sick tricks and flips on, of course) to maximise how much you can deliver. A bit less stressful than Kojima's joint, obviously, though elements are still there. Any money you earn from this gig can then be spent on restoring the shrine that you oh so love, which falls onto the sim side of things with the ability to fully customise how the shrine looks.

There are also a whole heap of minigames to perform that helps you get to know the locals. I'm talking baseball, sumo wrestling, working in a sushi restaurant and, of course, fishing. You can see bits of that in the launch trailer above, which comes with as 2010s an anime opening song you could wish for with some animation so good it makes me want an adaptation of the game. In time, perhaps! You can pick it up on Steam right here.

#3777. "Art, including characters, terrain, animations, cutscenes and UI" Bandai Namco and Monolith Soft helped out with Ocarina of Time on Switch 2

Xenoblade series developer Monolith Soft and Bandai Namco Studios have been listed as support studios for the Switch 2 version of Ocarina of Time, working on elements of the title such as "art, including characters, terrain, animations, cutscenes and UI". Special thanks to both companies appear in the credits for the newly-launched game (as you can see below) and a statement released by Bandai Namco Studios confirms its involvement, too.

"We were commissioned to produce some of the visual assets and artwork, including characters, environments, animations, cutscenes, and UI elements, for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, a Nintendo Switch 2 game released by Nintendo Co., Ltd. on 5th November, 2026," reads a translated release from Bandai Namco Studio reads.

Of course, this isn't the first time we've seen Bandai Namco Studios' talents leveraged to help with Nintendo games: the publisher and its internal studios worked closely with Nintendo as a co-developer on the long-awaited Metroid Prime 4, and we know the studios are listed as co-developer for first-party Switch 2 titles like Mario Kart World and Splatoon Raiders. Typically, the work carried out by Bandai Namco comes from one of two dedicated internal studios that are contracted specifically to work with Nintendo: Studio 2 and Studio S. You can see a full list of the games Bandai Namco's support studios have worked on here. You'll note there are many Nintendo first-party titles listed here, going back to 2012 and Mario Kart 8. In late 2025, Nintendo acquired Bandai Namco Studios Singapore from the publisher, renaming the company Nintendo Studios Singapore.

"Alongside great judgement and clever tweaks, this astonishing remake has a proper ace up its sleeve," wrote our reviewer, Christian Donlan, in his five-star review of the Switch 2 game last week. "This is Ocarina as it's always been, as timeless and intricate, but it also has a vibrancy and clarity that makes it feel like it was just created last Wednesday."

If - somehow! - you've already gobbled up most of the game and you're keen to play it again, you will be pleased to know that Master Quest code has been found in datamined files for the title, suggesting DLC may well be on the way in the not-too-distant future.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an affair with one Alice Huang on Sunday; someone suspected of being a Chinese spy by US authorities. Trump has since spoken on the matter, saying he asked Jensen whether he knew she was a spy (he says he didn't) and offered words of support for his pal.

Trump told reporters, "I know the FBI is looking into it", and he said, "I think he'll [Huang] be in good shape." (via BBC)

Trump reportedly asked Huang if he had "any idea she was a spy", and Huang reportedly said he had "no idea."

Reportedly, Trump was given an indication that a Chinese spy was targeting Jensen Huang last year, and when a reporter asked if he regrets not acting on that briefing, he said, "No, I don't think so. I think he's an honourable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it."

Trump seemed to express sympathy for the Nvidia CEO, whilst also bragging about how advanced the company's Blackwell architecture is.

"He's got a chip that's 10 years advanced… because of the complexity, the Blackwell can't even be copied".

Trump continues, saying, "He's an amazing guy. I just hope there's no problem. If there is a problem, we'll let you know about it."

This week has been a rough one for Nvidia, with a few hundred billion dollars coming off the company's value, and law firms circling, looking to get in on the cash flow. Law firms such as Rosen Law Firm and Schall, Brown & Schwartz are reportedly urging investors to cover losses by claiming Nvidia is guilty of false and/or misleading statements and a failure to disclose key information.

Nvidia had previously denied the romantic connection between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang (no relation) before the information went public. Nvidia also vouched for Megaspeed, which is a Singaporean data centre company that Alice Huang is reportedly connected to.

Megaspeed has also been accused of and denies claims of chip smuggling, which is a lucrative business in China, a country that lacks the very latest AI chips from American-based companies.

As is ever the case, it will likely be some time before we have all the details, but it certainly doesn't look great for the game company turned AI company in the interim.

#3775. Skyrim lead designer hopes Sentinel will finally solve The Elder Scrolls' ladder problem

For such a simple, straightforward real-world object, ladders have been the bane of game developers' existence since the early days of the industry. And Bethesda's The Elder Scrolls Series is certainly no stranger to that struggle.

While we may be years away from the release of The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel, the recent title reveal reignited conversations about what longtime fans hope to see from it. That includes former Bethesda developers, such as Skyrim lead designer and Bethesda veteran Bruce Nesmith, who picked ladders as one thing he hopes Sentinel actually figures out.

If you're unfamiliar, ladders in Skyrim work in a weird way. You don't animatedly climb up and down them, but rather the character simply teleports from one end to the other. Speaking to The Examined Game (via GamesRadar+), Nesmith said that Skyrim's approach "really limits the art team in terms of how you can do multi-layer [levels]".

"It seems simple, it seems stupid, but you don't climb up and down ladders," said Nesmith. "All the ladders in Skyrim, you click on the ladder, poof, you're at the top or you have to climb a stair.

"But to do ladders, you have to deal with a whole host of questions which our programmers very legitimately put in front of us and said, 'You give me answers to these, I'll tell you how much programming time it's going to take to make them.' And you know, that caused problems right there."

Nesmith then pointed out the hidden complexity of creating functioning ladders in games, and the scenarios developers have to anticipate and account for, especially in a game as dynamic as an Elder Scrolls title.

"So, I'm halfway up a ladder, and [an] NPC decides to climb down it. What happens?" Nesmith posited. "The NPC has to have AI that will adjust for that. Does the player go through the NPC? Is he blocked by the NPC? Does the NPC stay on the ladder? Does the NPC go back up and know to wait and then come back down?

"And I'm just scratching the surface of some of the problems they brought up. So, it seems simple, and other games have climbing ladders, but we chose to put our efforts into other things to make them better rather than deal with that. So, I'd like to see Bethesda finally come around to making ladders a reality where you're actually climbing them and make the world feel a little more immersive."

While we know very little about Sentinel right now - much less how it's going to solve the ladder problem -that hasn't stopped fans from speculating about a number of topics, including what they believe is going to be a split / alternate timeline setup.

Marathon’s large-scale December update is rapidly approaching, and it looks to be answering every player complaint thus far.

In a new trailer for the Symbiosis update, launching on Dec. 8, Bungie teased a number of promising-looking changes to the base game, including the new Runner Shell called Bishop, an expansion of the Perimeter map that’s now being overtaken with some sort of organic overgrowth, opening up new playable areas, and more.

The main attraction is the new PvE mode, Expedition, which Bungie describes as a “co-op PvE roguelite.” Players must work together to complete objectives and fight against AI enemies without having to deal with enemy players, as Bungie answers the call for the game’s most-requested feature.

Echoing Destiny’s Tower, Marathon will also be getting its own social space, called Limbo. It includes a firing range and a spot for players to gather and hang out with friends. It looks like a good place to test out all new weapons and gear coming in the update, including the Maverick hand cannon, throwing knife, hack grenade, and flamethrower.

The playable Bishop class, meanwhile, has some sort of throwing knife, super-jump, and an ultimate where it whips out a sword and dashes through enemies to deal damage, making for one of the more unique Runner Shells available in the game thus far.

As if that wasn’t already a chunky enough update, Dec. 8 will also bring about a beta test for the Deathmatch mode, offering a more traditional PvP experience that Bungie fans will be familiar with compared to the extraction game type this new Marathon was originally built around.

This update may as well be called Project Hail Mary for Marathon, because it’s obvious Bungie has thrown its all into bringing what players have been pining for since the game dropped in March. Will it be enough? I genuinely don’t know, especially with GTA 6 set to take over gamers’ schedules everywhere.

But Bungie is looking to entice players even further with another free week, allowing full access to the game for all players from Dec. 8 to 15 (progression remains if players purchase the game after that), along with a Crew Up event offering rewards for gamers to play with their friends.

In the end, I must give credit where it’s due. I thought Marathon was a great game to begin with, but it did not click with the masses, and Bungie has done a lot to try and rectify that. I hope it works out.

House House says that generative AI was not used anywhere else.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Big Walk developer House House has sparked a brand-new generative AI debate after revealing that it utilised LLMs "sparingly" during the final stretch of the game's development.

The revelation came in the hours following a statement from a handful of jurors participating in the Independent Games Festival awards. In the statement, it called out the "significant increase in the number of submitted games developed with generative AI tools," adding that it had "set off some fairly intense discussion and disagreement across the judge and jury pools."

The statement specifically called out AI-generated code, saying it was "not an exception," adding: "Programming is a creative discipline whose labour deserves the same respect we extend to any part of making a game. This extends to the past work used to train these models without the creators' consent."

While no game was specifically called out, as Aftermath reports, it didn't take long for word to spread that one particular title had caused so much of the debate: Big Walk, and the recent discovery that it had made use of generative AI during development.

House House's cooperative puzzler has been a huge hitter this year, striking a chord with many (myself included) and standing as a strong awards contender in what has been a relatively quiet year for videogames.

It's also developed by a team that is no stranger to taking strong stances, as evidenced by its decision to keep the game off Xbox consoles to support the pro-Palestinian Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions movement. Which makes it even more surprising, to some, that House House opted to utilise generative AI.

In the wake of the news, the developer has tacked on an AI statement to the Big Walk website's FAQ. "In the final stretch of Big Walk's development, LLMs were used sparingly by House House to help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs," it reads. "In some cases, snippets from LLM responses were copied as a starting point to be modified into game code—we'd estimate that well under 0.1% of Big Walk's code had anything to do with this usage, and generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game."

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

The statement offers an example of how this was put into practice—in this case, "about 10 lines of code" used to fix a problem that House House was apparently unable to rectify manually or by speaking directly to a Unity engineer.

As for why there was no AI disclosure on Steam, the developer notes that the platform "does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage"—Valve clarified that in January—adding: "We are posting this disclosure as it has become a matter of public interest."

House House says that its statement "is not an endorsement of, or argument for, the use of AI tools, however minimal," before closing with: "Big Walk was developed without an internal AI usage policy in place, and we consider that lack of policy a failure. We will work to have a more comprehensive policy going forward."

#3772. Nintendo's legendary Kirby designer Masahiro Sakurai weighs in on gen-AI, saying "it has yet to gain my trust" but not to reject it completely

"Doing nothing is probably not the right approach."

Masahiro Sakurai, the designer behind many iconic Nintendo franchises such as Super Smash Bros. and several Kirby titles, has weighed in on the ongoing discussion of generative-AI use in game development.

At an event celebrating the release of his new book - Masahiro Sakurai’s Thoughts on Games - the veteran director told Famitsu he hasn't and currently isn't using the technology to make games, noting that the role of a designer is to generate ideas.

"It has yet to gain my trust," Sakurai said via DeepL machine translation. Regarding graphical use specifically, he added that, "It must not amount to exploitation of any kind," and that "for the time being, we can produce better results by coming up with ideas ourselves".

But Sakurai is wary of rejecting gen-AI completely, saying "making games today is far too difficult", with some games "running at a loss even after selling millions of copies". A company in that position may go under if it does not change its stance on generative-AI, he suggested. "Doing nothing is probably not the right approach," he said, but "where and how to use it" is a complex topic with a lot of uncertainties. Sakurai is taking "a slow-paced approach" for now.

Outside of regular industry layoffs, the use of generative-AI in games has been the most controversial topic amongst developers and players. Some argue it's already being used in multiple development disciplines, notably programming and writing code. Others, such as Shigeru Miyamoto, are more sceptical of the technology's capabilities, especially when it comes to the more creative and art-driven parts of game development.

#3771. Marvel Cosmic Invasion gets the replay value it needed at launch with new roguelite Dr. Doom DLC

When I reviewed Marvel Cosmic Invasion at launch last December, I enjoyed the game quite a bit as an old-school beat ’em up, but lamented its lack of replay value.

About 11 months later, that replay value has arrived in its new DLC, The Siege of Castle Doom. The expansion adds both Doctor Doom and Invisible Woman as playable characters, but also a whole new game mode for players to group up and have fun with. And it’s carried by the industry’s favorite new old reliable, roguelite mechanics.

The Siege of Castle Doom tasks players with mowing down waves of foes, including new Doombot enemies, and moving from room to room by choosing where to go next, similar to classics in the genre like Hades. Doors within Castle Doom have different icons on them, and they offer different rewards, but in the end it’s all about slaying enemies as quickly as posible.

But there’s also a Siege Counter on the bottom right of the screen that fills up as you play, making enemies stronger and quicker. Once that gauge fills, the run is over, and you have to start from scratch once again. This puts a lot of urgency on killing enemies as fast as possible to gain batteries to charge up your upgrades, fighting bosses from the base game to lower the doom gauge and keep yourself alive long enough to face the final boss, Victor Von Doom himself.

But there’s also a sense of progression in the mode in that you use charges gain to unlock permanent stat upgrades and very special unlocks. These include powerful, game-changing modifiers like gaining an extra life instead of a second hero, or equipment like Vibranium (25 bonus HP for 10 seconds) or SHIELD Turret (summon a HeliCarrier turret for 7 seconds).

The DLC mode differs from the base game in that enemies drop batteries that you use to charge up an item on the bottom left of the screen. Filling up that gauge rewards you with a choice of a buff (Offensive, Defensive, or Tactical), as shown in the screenshot above, making each run feel unique, and this is the main mechanic behind clearing the mode. Kill enemies, grab batteries, charge up abilities, and make it to the final boss fight.

The randomness of a run of Siege makes it fun, like any roguelite before it, but the gameplay does not reinvent the wheel by any means. This is the same fun Marvel Cosmic Invasion combat, now more replayable and with two more playable heroes (which is exactly what I wished for at launch), and both are quite powerful.

Doom is a tankier, slower playable, using melee attacks combined with magic green lightning to clear the screen, including a projectile that debuffs enemies. Invisible Woman, meanwhile, moves a bit quicker, has a ranged attack that can freeze enemies in place, and can fly, making her my favorite of the two new heroes. She can also go invisible, of course, giving her a few seconds of safety from enemy attacks. But make no mistake, Doom hits hard, so he’s worth trying out as well.

This DLC is genuinely a good time that adds on to an already-fun game, and for $7.99, worth the price of admission, because it’s easily replayable and enjoyable especially when you bring a Marvel fan friend along for the ride.

"We felt that experiencing that was the best way to introduce the origins"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Capcom's modern Resident Evil remakes are fantastic entry points for one of the most beloved survival horror series of all time, but it's always felt weird that the very first 1996 game still hasn't been given the full-blown third-person RE Engine treatment. Yes, there's a remake from 2002, but it's way more faithful to the original game than the much more recent remakes of Resident Evil 2, 3, and 4, featuring the classic tank controls and static camera from the series' origin. Basically, if you want to start Resident Evil with the first game in the series, you have to deal with quite a few design foundations that'll feel seriously dated if you're unfamiliar. Like ink ribbons. You don't want ink ribbons, trust me.

With how successful the Resident Evil remakes have been, it may seem inevitable that Capcom revisits the very first game. But while rumors suggest there's already a new RE1 early in development, there's been no official announcement or even heavily substantiated reporting to add weight to those rumors. As to why Capcom didn't choose Resident Evil as the obvious starting point for its newer remakes, longtime series producer Jun Takeuchi says the company worried it wouldn't resonate with a modern audience.

"The reason we didn't choose Resident Evil 1 as the first remake is because it's such a stoic game," Takeuchi says in a new book celebrating the series' 30th anniversary (translation via Fandom). "Because it focuses so heavily on the horror derived from its stoicism, we were concerned that it might not resonate with today's game fans."

As is always the case with second-hand translations, it's hard to pin down the exact intent behind translated words like "stoic," but Resident Evil 1 definitely has a distinct vibe and slower pace than newer games in the series. Speaking of which, Takeuchi says the iconic opening sequence from Resident Evil 2, which sets up the mass infection of Raccoon City, is basically where everything kicks off anyway.

"Furthermore, the Raccoon City incident is essentially the starting point of the Resident Evil saga, so we felt that experiencing that was the best way to introduce the origins," he says.

I definitely don't disagree. Resident Evil 2 is arguably the most classic version of Resident Evil you can experience, whether that's the 1998 original or the 2019 remake. That said, as a lifelong fan and noted tank control hater, I would love to see a modern reimagining of the game that started it all.

Where does your favorite land on our ranking of the best Resident Evil games?

#3769. Activision cracking down on popular Call of Duty: Warzone app that basically constituted cheating

"Lobby shopping" is what Call of Duty: Warzone players have been calling the ability to check the skill level of players in a lobby prior to joining it, enabling them to pass on those that include a lot of tough competition.

There are several ways players, notably Twitch streamers and content creators, have been able to do that over the years. But the use of one app in particular - Warzone Agent - has been considered by many to be cheating, and Activision is finally doing something about it.

Alongside the launch of Modern Warfare 4's version of Warzone and the game's first season of post-launch content, Call of Duty's anti-cheat team Ricochet has announced it's officially cracking down on Warzone Agent.

"Yesterday, we began taking action against Warzone Agent, a paid, unauthorised third party tool that lets users lobby shop in Warzone," the developer revealed in a post on X. "Ricochet anti-cheat will block players attempting to load the software and instruct them to unload it before accessing multiplayer."

Having the ability to cherrypick the lobby with the lowest-skilled players possible bypasses the game's matchmaking algorithm, potentially ruining the game for the dozens of other players in the match. Historically, content creators have used the app (and other methods) to post impressive kill records.

The developer added in a follow-up message that: "Using unauthorised software to manipulate the player experience violates Activision terms of use and leaves your account and hardware subject to enforcement." The language seems to stop just short of outright confirming those players using Warzone Agent will be banned.

As part of this crackdown, Ricochet reiterated its stance on boosting - artificially increasing (or decreasing) one's skill rating - saying that it too is considered cheating. "Receiving a boost, having another player log in to boost your account, or purchasing a boosted account are all against policy," the developer said.

"Boosting services flood lobbies with low effort accounts used to farm XP and complete challenges. Those accounts can later be sold as Ranked Play ready, directly feeding the cheating marketplace."

More than 20,000 boosting-related accounts have been removed since the launch of Modern Warfare 4, according to the developer, and Ricochet will "continue to apply pressure" in this area.

The quality of multiplayer was a particular highlight in Eurogamer's review of Modern Warfare 4, in which Dom Peppiatt lauded the complexity of weapon handling, which works without taking away from accessibility of the gunplay.

Silent Hill: Townfall's St. Amelia is a singularly unnerving location, especially if, like me, you are blessed with the good fortune to be a Scot. It's a fictional place, but one that a lot of us are intimately familiar with, even as it's twisted by fog and trauma. It's a nightmare, and like most nightmares it's powerfully relatable.

When I spoke with director Jon McKellan at Gamescom, we talked a lot about Scottishness and authenticity, which St. Amelia has in spades. And with the game now out in the wilds, we've reconvened—this time joined by art director Paul Abbott—to dig deeper into the town's origins, and the process that brought it to life.

Screen Burn knew it wanted to create St. Amelia, and it had a clear vision for the town right at the start. "We knew where we wanted to draw reference from—lots of Scottish coastal towns, island towns, stuff like that," McKellan tells me. "Once you've played through the story, I think the things that have happened to St. Amelia, it's very much because of who they are and where they are. So it was always a fundamental part of the story that it was the type of town it was."

"We realised that leaning into things was going to make things much more authentic."

But what wasn't locked down was St. Amelia's location. "What wasn't clear right away was whether we were actually going to say that it was a Scottish town or just a Northern European town, and kind of leave it very vague." It didn't take long for Screen Burn to settle on making it more specific, however. "We realised that leaning into things was going to make things much more authentic."

The original pitch to Konami described it as a small fishing village with Scottish heritage—something that should feel familiar and nostalgic to Scots, but bizarre to players from outside of the UK. "It should feel like a very new type of environment," McKellan adds.

After 27 years of both publishing and developing Silent Hill games, you might expect Konami to be extremely protective of the horror series, but McKellan says the publisher proved to be pretty hands-off—it was fully onboard with Screen Burn's concept.

"They knew we were passionate about striving for authenticity," he says, "not just in visuals but in the general feel of things—and that having a Scottish team build a Scottish town was the right way to go. Both Konami and Annapurna would regularly play and provide feedback, of course, but I think what was really surprising from the get-go was how aligned we all were on our general ideas and pitch."

It's surprising, given how much of a big deal Silent Hill has once more become for Konami—there's the assumption that big publishers like to meddle a wee bit, or leave developers with challenging restrictions. "It's such a rare joy to work with teams that welcome experimentation and exploration," McKellan adds, "especially on a franchise as big as this."

Konami's faith paid off. When I first stepped into St. Amelia, it was like being hurled back 30 years. The wallpaper, furniture, a thousand little touches, all reminding me of what Scotland looked like when I was wee. "I think pretty much anyone that's kind of grown up in the UK or been here a lot will find something recognisable within St. Amelia somewhere," says McKellan, "whether it's shop signs or your granny's kitchen. You'll find something to hook onto, but then for people who are not from the UK, it's somewhere they've never seen before."

These tiny familiar or alien touches, depending on what part of the world you live in, aren't merely set dressing. The old TVs and crimes against interior decorating ground Townfall with their mundanity, which makes the horror rug pull all the more effective.

"Whether it's Silent Hill-style horror or sci-fi horror, the more grounded and believable something can be, the more it affects you when it goes wrong," says McKellan. "So if you can buy into the world, if it's familiarity or detail or touch points that people can relate to—all of that starts to build a subconscious picture. And when you turn it on its head and flip it, it becomes all the more unsettling. If everything was completely crazy, then nothing's crazy."

It helped that St. Amelia already kind of existed—or versions of it, at least.

"We toured all over Scotland," says McKellan, "and some of North England as well. We went down to North Berwick, down that east coast, and went up to Shetland, which obviously had a lot of parallels, up in Lerwick, especially for the story we told."

Lerwick is the UK's most northern town, more than 100 miles away from the mainland. It's not particularly easy to get to, so Screen Burn only visited it once, but you can see a lot of it in St. Amelia—that cosiness juxtaposed to how isolated it is.

St. Monans, on the Fife coast, was another major influence. You can tell even at just a glance: the coloured houses on the waterfront, the reliance on fishing, the sense, in specific locations, that time has stood still. There are buildings and streets that Screen Burn replicated in St. Amelia almost exactly.

"It's this tiny little pocket town off to the side that a lot of people don't really talk about," says McKellan. "There's not a lot there, but those are the kind of places that captured the history better. Like, hadn't moved on quite so much, so you could kind of see how things used to be a little bit clearer."

It was perfect for Townfall. Pretty, but not lavish; not well known, but familiar. And it's got a bit of bite to it. St. Monans was, after all, named after a Christian missionary murdered during a Danish raid more than a thousand years ago.

You could kind of see how things used to be a little bit clearer.

But the atmosphere of St. Amelia is not entirely unique to Scotland. Abbot is English, and a lot of St. Amelia is drawn from his experiences and local haunts. "I grew up in the north of England, '70s and '80s, and it's quite a bleak place. And there's a lot of that in the game."

As Abbott points out, St. Amelia also captures the British horror films and TV shows of the '70s and '80s as well, "where you've got these empty towns that have just recently been lived in, but there's just this eeriness you recognise, and there's no one about."

Even though there were a lot of references that Screen Burn was able to draw from, St. Amelia feels so cohesive because a lot of these wee towns are already so similar. When the studio narrowed down what it needed St. Amelia to be (not too big, not too touristy), that left it with a shortlist of towns that had a great deal in common.

Its island setting also informed a lot of the artistic and design decisions that Screen Burn had to make, "even down to what stone would be available to build these buildings," says McKellan.

"I think that helped, didn't it?" Abbott adds. "That direction of, well, it's a small island, they've only got a certain amount of materials on that island to work with, and so that just limits your palette, so it ties everything together."

So St. Amelia was locked in very early on, but the path to bringing it to life wasn't straightforward, says McKellan. "A lot of it was evolving with the story, with the gameplay, kind of back and forth."

One thing that stayed the course, however, was that players would be exploring it in a first-person perspective. "From the original pitch it was always first-person," says McKellan. "We knew that searching and exploring the environment, and learning about the town in that way, was a key pillar, and you just don't build the same connection when your camera is five meters away from everything all the time.

"We felt with St. Amelia being 'the star of the show' we should let you really get in about it, and search those cabinets and drawers as you would in real life. It really informed how we built the town, as with no camera to accommodate over the players shoulders, we didn't have to compromise in accuracy or scale. Everything is a 1:1 match with its real-life counterparts. None of our doors are three times the height they should be just to let the camera through."

To create something that so overtly matched reality involved a lot of travel and a lot of snapping.

Because the town is based on real places, Screen Burn didn't need to do much concept art. But it did have to take a lot of photographs all over Scotland. "I'd drive around looking for fog, and take loads of concept photography because we didn't have to paint over it," McKellan says. "It exists. It's there. We can just draw direct reference. So we were driving around Scotland, taking a lot of photographs and building what the kind of visual identity of a town should be, but when it came to the layout, how it fits together, that was a much slower, more experimental process".

One of the first things the team did, McKellan recalls, was figure out all the metrics—"how big should things be, especially in first-person"—which involved using LiDAR to scan entire streets.

"We'd walk around with our iPhones or with our SLRs," he says, "and take thousands of photographs, stitch them together, and build this 3D scanned version in Unreal that we could walk around, and that would give us 1:1 measurements for everything. So we could find out how wide the roads are, how deep the curb is, stuff that most people would never ever think about."

It's a lot simpler to create modern cities—which are often laid out in a grid. That's not how an old fishing village looks. "They all radiate out from the port. So the road patterns are never a grid; they're never simple. Everything's a curve on top of a curve, which is a nightmare to make in videogames. So we had lots of difficult decisions to make in terms of how authentic we'd stick to it, and we decided to go all-in, for better or worse, and make the layout of this town make as much sense as it should in pursuit of authenticity over game design."

McKellan remembers it being a "really long process" to make it feel like a real town while still working as a location for a survival horror game.

But the realism actually worked well with the demands of a survival horror game, he notes. The small streets, buildings squashed up against each other, there's a thin line between quaint and oppressive. "What it means is that we knew that even when you're outside in the fog, you're still going to feel a sense of claustrophobia, and you're still going to feel lost. These towns are really sweet and cute on a summer's day, but when you stick monsters and fog in there, it suddenly becomes a labyrinth, even when you're outdoors in the open."

Despite the town often feeling claustrophobic, players were still given quite a lot of freedom of movement, and that can be a challenge when designing a horror game, where pacing is everything. So Screen Burn needed to identify where to limit that freedom, and how to nudge players in an appropriate direction.

When Simon first arrives in St. Amelia, players aren't able to run, because Screen Burn wanted to slowly unfurl the town and build up its thick atmosphere. And the game is filled with subtle cues and other bits and pieces that subtly guide the player without being too obtrusive. It might be through the use of colour—but no yellow paint—or the composition of a specific scene, or just the lighting. There's gating, too, like locked doors that require a bit of backtracking to open, but after which you're able to create a shortcut.

"Ultimately we try to respect the players' freedom to explore as they want," McKellan says, "and if they want to spend 15 minutes looking at every shop window on the way into town, they can, and it's just up to us to make sure that that doesn't completely fall apart if they do. So yeah, there's only so much you can do in exchange for that player freedom."

There are so many nostalgic flourishes that I couldn't help but slowly snoop around, admiring mundane props that brought St. Amelia to life, like the familiar guide dog charity box, or even just little notices in shop windows. In many cases these are real objects that were scanned or, in the case of notices and the protest placards you find in the town square, initially created by hand.

You've just got to remember what it was like and then recreate it.

Location visits naturally helped with this, and as McKellan told me at Gamescom, the team found scans of old '90s Argos catalogues that helped them create furniture and electronics that fit the era. But naturally there are limits to what can be found online.

"Memory is a big thing," says Abbot, "because you can't just go and search on the internet for '90s packaging design, because there's not a lot of it there. You've just got to remember what it was like and then recreate it. We put a lot of effort into the packaging and also understanding technology and what people were doing with it at the time. So in the family clinic, there's some Word art on the wall. You can't do that in Word now, but we remembered what it looked like, so we just recreated it because people were doing it. It was like, yeah, we can make our words 3D and wobbly now."

The problem with looking for '80s and '90s inspiration online is that so much of the aesthetic of that era has been infected by America and Hollywood. If you were around for the '80s in the UK, you almost certainly would not have been surrounded by neon and vaporwave.

"Especially in the UK, it's just grey," says McKellan. "Grey, wet, dull. Everything's navy. Very concrete. Once you get past the early 2000s, what you find on the internet is very much the stylised version of it, and the reference actually just stops existing. You've got to literally dig out photo albums from your granny's house and start searching through things that way."

All the photos and paintings that you'll find in St. Amelia are real, too. Screen Burn used old family photos to decorate the town's homes, created with analogue cameras, long before the rise of digital photography. Many of the paintings, meanwhile, were created by McKellan's wife's great grandad, Andrew Hall, who died in 1953 but is in the game's credits.

"He was born in the 1800s and was not a famous painter in any way," McKellan says. "He was just someone who did it as a hobby. And then a few years back, we found this collection of paintings that he'd done, and they were just perfect working class Glaswegian hobbyist paintings. And then they become a big part of the game, giving things that authentic feel. Instead of trying to paint a bunch of images that look like paintings from the era, we actually just found them and used them."

As Abbott says, "You just can't fake that stuff." And even before I knew their origin, I spent a lot of time in-game admiring them. Not because they are incredible works of art—though they are undeniably good—but because they all evoke such a strong sense of place and time. "His drawings and his paintings are beautiful because you can just see the way that they've evolved over time, and he does stuff in them where it's like, there's no way I could fake that."

McKellan's wife, Lee, is Screen Burn's art producer, and the team also got their kids involved, giving them paper and pens and telling them to go to town, resulting in all the kids' drawings that you'll encounter. Multiple generations of family members ended up contributing to the game, and together, all these little touches build up to create a place that doesn't simply feel real, it feels human.

Naturally, this creates a disturbing juxtaposition when you are faced with something inhuman—not just the monsters, but corporations as well. The little houses, the post office, the local shop, they all share a space with ugly modern buildings funded by CEG, a corporation that looms over Townfall, and the reason you see all the protest signs at the start of the game. And unlike the monsters, this is all very true to life.

"Having things like CEG funding part of the health center is a very real thing," says McKellan. "When companies move in and take over a town, they will invest in local infrastructure because they have to. It's usually part of the condition of the deal. If you're going to build a giant warehouse in a rural town somewhere, it's going to give most of the people there in that town a job. Then you've probably got to invest in infrastructure and pay back to the community a little bit. All of those things help bring a believability to it and understand the sort of tension between all the different aspects of a small town and how fragile it can be."

Discovering this is also part of the journey, with Townfall's deliberate pace revealing more and more modernity as you move through the game—you start to really see the impact CEG had on St. Amelia, especially in places like Clara Woods, an austere residential area covered in concrete.

"I really wanted to illustrate the difference between a traditional fishing village town that can sustain itself with tourism," says McKellan, "and then what these big companies can and do to communities, and how it changes over time … so it really helps sell the contrast, sort of almost like a before and after, pre-CEG and post-CEG in a way."

But how do proper monsters fit into this very real town with very real problems? Thanks to Silent Hill's penchant for horrors born from trauma, it's actually a pretty natural fit.

"We tried to follow the same rules that Silent Hill's established over the years," says McKellan, "which is that these creatures are visual manifestations of the protagonists' inner demons, or some way connected to them, and they mean something to them, even if it's not explicit."

Screen Burn's take on these monsters is more grounded than usual, too—"more normal looking," as McKellan puts it. "The guy that Zoe sees, the Sorrowful, he looks like a normal guy, and he's in his pants, and he's got burns all over him. It's far less surreal than what people are maybe used to seeing. Though it is still very surreal: the guy opens his chest and needles come out. But on the face of it, at a glance, it's a guy in his pants standing in a hallway, and you're not quite sure what to make of that."

The team wanted to avoid filling St. Amelia with creatures that were immediately repellant—at least in terms of their silhouette. At a distance, they often just look like people. Because they are—they are representations of the residents of St. Amelia who have gone through something horrific, whether it's a great loss or medical mistreatment.

St. Amelia's Widows, which you'll face when you're playing as Richard, are another great example of this. Designed by Abbott, their silhouette suggests a woman wearing a veil—a woman in mourning. But then you get near them and see that the veil is, as Abbot says, "a slimy piece of flesh instead, and then you get the Silent Hill sort of revulsion when you look close". The Widows are also wrapped up in the protest signs that were used to call out CEG after the death of their husbands. They are terrifying and tragic in equal measure.

Townfall's monsters are twisted shadows of victims, and frankly I hated killing them. And that's the point. It's why the game encourages stealth, McKellan explains. "When you're playing as Richard, if you kill everyone or close to everyone, an achievement pops up which is called 'Missing the Point Entirely'. Because you're basically charging around and murdering all of these Widows with a shotgun instead of listening to them, instead of taking note of what they're trying to show you."

And there are layers of symbolism. When you see a burned man, you immediately think that represents someone who maybe dies in a fire, but why is he in his pants? Why are there only burns on one part of his body? "There's a lot of reasons for all that," says McKellan, "and people are slowly starting to pick away at the layers of it, and it's all very much intentional."

The monsters and stealth also informed parts of St. Amelia's design. Once Screen Burn realised that a specific part of the town was going to have some sort of combat or stealth scenario, it returned to the location to add additional touches. "What might be a front door of a building that's closed might turn into one of those storm door hiding spots, for example," McKellan says. "Or we might need to open the space up so that the players get somewhere to hide, and we'd take a building away and replace it with a garden adjacent to another one."

It was important to provide all of these opportunities for stealth in a way that didn't come across as "too obvious or so gamey," McKellan adds, so there was a back and forth between departments as the level design evolved. And that was a challenge. "Some things do become contrived. Like half-height cover, we'd have to think about what kind of objects would be things you could hide behind on a street, and it turns out that there's not a lot of them—there's not a lot of places to hide on an open street."

One of the solutions Screen Burn settled on was adverts stuck to railings—signs for tours and shops and so on. They're not incongruous and if you crouch you can hide behind them. But for all of them, Screen Burn found a precedent first, some kind of reference to base it on, and only then would it go into the game.

When stealth fails and the monsters are coming at you, that's when the guns come out. But that wasn't always the case. Firearms aren't a particularly British thing outside of shotgun-wielding farmers, and in 1997 two consecutive governments, one Conservative and one Labour, created tighter restrictions on firearms, which ultimately led to a ban on most types of handguns. This was prompted by a school shooting the year before, in Dunblane, Scotland. It never happened again. But Townfall occurs just before these events.

"We're right on the edge in terms of 'historical accuracy,' as shotguns and pistols were still around in early 1996, although extremely rare," says McKellan. "For some time we had no firearms in the game and the flare gun was the only ranged weapon, but it felt too limiting to not have any option to 'take a piece off the chess board' from relative safety. It just felt just too punishing. Melee is effective but risky, it brings a different proposition to the player than ranged."

But even with St. Amelia needing to support melee brawls, shooting and stealth, it never starts to look like a combat arena. It's always just a town.

I'm still pretty stunned by how meticulous St. Amelia, and Townfall more broadly, feels while I'm playing. I'm a big scaredy cat, so I don't go out of my way to explore in most horror games (which is probably why I often end up out of ammo and resources, and very dead), but I couldn't help myself here.

The care and attention to detail demands to be seen and admired. But that also heightens the horror—seeing all these awful things happening in a town that could be my own. Not a space station. Not somewhere in the US or Japan, but so close to home I could take a bus there and be back in time to feed the dog.

Horror is best when it's personal. And St. Amelia really makes it feel so personal. For me, but even more so for Screen Burn and McKellan. So what's the scariest part of St. Amelia for the man who orchestrated its creation?

"It's Clara Woods," says McKellan. "Mainly because it definitely hits closest to home for me personally. My first apartment was essentially one of the flats you see on that first road into Clara Woods, with all the dead lying in the streets. While I've not seen that many people lying on the road, it was a very rough part of town to live and a rough time of life—I've genuinely felt like I was being hunted in those places for real, so if some of that horror comes through we've done our job correctly."

#3766. Marvel Rivals’ Doomsday-themed season 11 brings Nightcrawler into the fold, and Dracula soon

Doom is here. But first, a blue, religious mutant who can teleport all over the battlefield.

Nightcrawler has been confirmed as the newest Marvel Rivals hero, launching alongside season 11 this Friday. The X-Men member looks to be a Strategist who can use his teleportation ability to get teammates out of harm’s way.

“Two timelines, the present and the future, are on a course for an Incursion,” the update teases. “New York and Nueva York are about to collide head-on! Will they find a solution in separation, or will each look out for its own interests? How will the heroes’ actions affect the ambitions of the two Doctor Dooms? How will a pious saint with the visage of a demon and the exiled king trapped in a foreign land shoulder the burden of saving two worlds?”

Here’s everything we know so far about the season 11 update hitting Marvel Rivals on Nov. 13.

BAMF! Kurt Wagner, otherwise known as the X-Men team member Nightcrawler, is the 55th hero to join Marvel Rivals, and the game’s 13th Strategist (healer). He looks to be a very agile hero, teleporting in and out of battle, healing allies and dealing damage with swords and his tail.

The end of the trailer teases that Dracula, waking from his slumber, will be the new hero in the 11.5 update in December, refuting leaks that it would be Doctor Doom.

It’s all about Doom these days, and rightfully so, as the iconic villain gets his shine in Avengers: Doomsday next month. This is the second birthday of Marvel Rivals, coming up in December, including an area in Times Square to play mini-games, exclusive anniversary-themed costumes, and more.

“Severe offenders” will face a year-long ban and account suspensions when it comes to hate speech in-game, according to NetEase. The team is cracking down on the community.

#3765. Rockstar's doing a GTA 6 launch 'festival' in Miami featuring a lot of presumably expensive musical stars

The next-level glamour of Grand Theft Auto 6's arrival continues with word that Rockstar is hosting a star-studded launch 'festival' for the game in Miami - the game's setting-by-a-different-name.

The event will feature two stages hosting live performances by musical artists both featured in the game and from those who are not. Cardi B is probably the headliner - my knowledge of popular music is creaking here - but there's also Travis Scott, Don Toliver, Kodak Black, Sofaygo, Ca7riel, and Paco Amoroso.

Meanwhile, GTA 6 soundtrack duo Justice are doing a DJ set, as are The Dare with Fcukers, which is a dangerous name to spell. Also appearing: Metro Boomin, Nick León with DJ Python, Propsa with Skream, Rauw and Friends, Suero, and Tainy.

The event is being hosted at event space Mana Wynwood, and the pre-sale lottery for tickets begins this week on Wednesday, 11th November. Tickets are limited to two a head.

The full soundtrack for GTA 6 is yet to be revealed, with only a handful of songs so far detailed - featuring Rauw, Ca7riel, Paco Amoroso, and Travis Scott, among others. But of course music and radio stations play a huge role in the series, and given the amount of time we'll be playing GTA 6 and listening to these songs, it may well provide a lucrative platform to be featured on.

Meanwhile, the cultural impact of GTA 6's imminent arrival continues with a takeover of swanky department store Selfridges in London, which has a custom Ferrari parked in a window and an extensive range of expensive merch to buy.

It's not all good news for Rockstar, though. The company is also fighting an employment tribunal in Scotland relating to the sudden firing of 31 staff from Rockstar North this time last year. Rockstar alleges this was done for gross misconduct reasons, whereas the fired staff maintain it was done in the name of union busting. The results of that hearing are expected close to GTA 6's release, on 19th November.

#3764. Side-By-Side Comparisons Show Breath Of The Wild‘s Fingerprints All Over The Ocarina Of Time Remake In The Best Way

The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the WildThe Legend of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time

There’s a new video out from GameXplain showing off differences in how certain locations appear between Breath of The Wild and the Switch 2 Ocarina of Time remake. The video features side-by-side comparisons of locations shared between the gamesâthe Temple of Time, Lake Hylia, Lon Lon Ranch, and more. And while there’s much to be said for the graphical improvements of Ocarina 4K Electric Boogaloo over BotW, what’s more fascinating is how the similarities reinforce the idea that the worlds of OoT and BotW, separated by different game mechanics and stories and thousands of in-world years, are nevertheless the same.

We know, thanks to the Hyrule Hystoria as well as any one of the many attempts by content creators to sort out the Zelda timeline, that Hyrule is one place. That despite the many games with their differing mythologies, including that time the world was totally flooded for like forever, we’ve always been in a singular Hyrule. But this video is perhaps the best illustration of what we’ve always, up to this point, had to take on faith.

Look at the Temple of Time. Yes, inÂ Breath of the Wild a whole faÃ§ade of the building has been shorn off by calamity and time, but looking at it, you could believe it’s the same structure that a distant ancestor of Link brought three spiritual stones to when he was little boy. The interiors of the buildings are slightly different, possibly indicating that these aren’t the same assets, but even if so, it’s hardly uncommon for buildings to be remodeled or restored, leaving them slightly changed from what they were.

I like the stories these similar but slightlyÂ differentÂ structures tell. Death Mountain stands tall in Ocarina of Time, but has been worn down to a nub in Breath of the Wild. And all that’s left of Lon Lon Ranch by the time Breath of the Wild occurs are a few long-abandoned remnants of the place that Malon and Talon once called home.

It’s really neat to see this kind of continuity. The Zelda series has obviously achieved that in other ways, too, like having the same characters pop up over and over, but to see it in the structures themselves is a nice little visual reminder that the worlds of these two very different games are really the same world, changed by time.

#3763. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang under investigation after admitting affair with alleged Chinese spy in company-wide email

"There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."

Nvidia's board of directors has launched an investigation into its own CEO Jensen Huang, after a report by the New York Times claimed he had been participating in an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Huang admitted to having an affair in a company-wide statement, apologising to his wife as well as to Nvidia employees. Following this acknowledgement, independent investigators are looking into whether or not he's been the target of a "foreign intelligence effort".

Per the New York Times article, the alleged spy was named as Megaspeed executive and Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang or Huang Le. Jensen Huang wrote in his internal letter: "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."

With regard to security concerns surrounding the CEO of US-based company Nvidia potentially sharing information with a spy, Huang confirmed that the Nvidia board of directors had initiated an investigation. He added: "I support the investigation and will cooperate fully." The Nvidia board has said it has "no reason to believe either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised."

Huang will remain CEO of Nvidia while the investigation is conducted. The New York Times report also claimed that US government officials did not believe Huang knew of Alice Huang's alleged intelligence activities for China.

Following the internal letter from Jensen Huang, Nvidia stock took a tumble from $162bn to $150bn. Nvidia, a juggernaut in the video game hardware industry, is also a key player in the global generative AI industry, which is currently carrying the US economy as other sectors struggle. The company is responsible for AI technology like DLSS 5, which generates lighting, shadows and more using generative AI.

Concerns around the Chinese AI sector passing the American industry has been a core argument against AI development slowdown or regulation, and it's also why Huang's affair may be a matter of national interest.

#3762. GTA 6 is the ‘most pre-ordered game in PlayStation history’ despite the fact it’s locked at 30FPS, even on PS5 Pro

Even a choppy frame rate can't stop the hype train.

It’s official, folks; Grand Theft Auto VI is now the most pre-ordered game of all time, and players who helped set that record can now start pre-loading it.

With over seven million pre-purchases and counting, GTA VI has been on track to become the most pre-ordered video game ever made for months. This morning, the official PlayStation account on X confirmed that GTA VI has finally reached that impressive milestone, formally dethroning Cyberpunk 2077, which held the title of “most pre-ordered game of all time” since its 2020 release.

Grand Theft Auto VI is the most pre-ordered game in PlayStation Store history!Mark the occasion with a video showcasing why GTAVI plays best on PS5Get ready for launch on November 19 by clearing PS5 storage space and pre-loading today: https://t.co/wTPa5E4DJY pic.twitter.com/WTQvHQs9cI

In a truly happy twist of fate, this groundbreaking moment synced up almost perfectly with Rockstar Games announcing through their website that GTA VI is now up for pre-loading. Anyone who’s already purchased a digital copy can now start downloading it to their console or PC, so it’ll be ready to play as soon as it releases on November 19, 2026.

As great as this news is, it also comes with a caveat. In the same post where they confirmed players can pre-load the game, Rockstar also explained that GTA 6 is locked at 30fps, even on the PlayStation 5 Pro, to ensure roughly the same quality across platforms.

Grand Theft Auto VI has been fully developed from the ground up to provide the best possible experience for the current generation of consoles, targeting 30 frames per second while pushing both platforms to their absolute limits to bring the vast and rich world of Leonida to life — while maintaining the density and visual fidelity of all its environments and inhabitants.

While plenty of gamers will be upset that they won’t be able to experience Leonida and all its unhinged beauty at 60fps, Rockstar confirmed that PS5 Pro owners will get a pretty crisp cut of the game thanks to PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution and higher ray-tracing support. It’s a small victory, but it’s a victory nonetheless.

In other happy news, Xbox CEO Asha Shar announced that GTA VI will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming on both the Xbox Series X|S and Xbox One as part of a newly unveiled “ten-year strategic partnership” with Take-Two

Today marks the first step in our new 10-year strategic partnership with Take-Two. GTA VI, already the most pre-ordered game ever on Microsoft Store, will be playable on XBOX One through cloud gaming when it launches on November 19. https://t.co/WTtRs6plZx

As sad as some people are about the hard 30fps limit, it’s clear that the GTA hype storm isn’t going anywhere. So if you’re one of the millions who’ve already downloaded GTA VI, now’s the perfect time to get it onto your system.

Developer of entertainment products and pillar of the global economy Rockstar has announced that Grand Theft Auto 6, its much-ballyhooed upcoming Bonnie and Clyde simulator, will be targeting 30 frames per second on consoles. Coincidentally, "on consoles" is the only place Rockstar has currently announced the game is releasing, so GTA 6 is a 30-fps-or-bust experience for the foreseeable future.

"Grand Theft Auto 6 has been fully developed from the ground up to provide the best possible experience for the current generation of consoles, targeting 30 frames per second while pushing both platforms to their absolute limits to bring the vast and rich world of Leonida to life", say the boys and girls in Edinburgh, while offering a little sweet treat to PlayStation 5 Pro owners in the form of PSSR (PlayStation of Soviet Socialist Republics—no, wait, sorry, PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution) support and ray-traced shadows.

Why am I telling you this on PC Gamer dot com? Partially because the traffic gods would beat me with a roll of pennies in a sock if I passed up an opportunity to write about GTA 6, but mostly because I'm very smug, and wish to subject other people to that.

Let's be real, the odds that GTA 6 was gonna target 60 fps on the box you have under your TV were always slim to none, but hearing it makes me feel more vindicated in my choice to wait for the game to hit PC than ever. I'm sure Rockstar's tech magi will make it a very nice 30 fps indeed, but my TV has 120 hertz in it. My monitor? 144, which I gather is kind of on the low end these days.

When it comes time for me to luxuriate in the lights of Leonida, I want to do it with maximum butteriness, I want all the bells and whistles set to 'on', and I want to do it on a proper gaming platform (German Linux). I'm excited to hear people's reports about what this game's actually like when it finally hits consoles in just over a week, but personally? I've never been happier about my choice to wait for GTA 6's inevitable but unannounced PC port.

#3760. Anticipated Warhammer 40K tactical RPG Dark Heresy gets a release date

Owlcat Games has revealed a release date for its tactical role-playing sequel Warhammer 40,000: Dark Heresy. The game arrives 28th January, 2027 on PC, PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series S/X. A Switch 2 release date will be provided "at a later date", a press release says.

Warhammer 40,000: Dark Heresy follows the good work laid down by Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader a couple of years ago. "Rogue Trader nails the 40k setting and provides an appropriately massive narrative filled with meaty tactical combat, though some bugs and poor performance hold it back," wrote Caeyln Ellis in Eurogamer's Warhammer 40,000 Rogue Trade review.

Dark Heresy changes things by casting you as an Inquisitor and tasking you with hunting down heretics and purging the world of dark influences, as one is wont to do in the 41st century, it seems. And developer Owlcat has apparently overhauled many of the systems underpinning the adventure.

There's a beta that's been running for a while that offers a complete first Act to try, and it's accessible if you buy a Founders edition of the game. This beta, incidentally, disappears 7th January, when Owlcat prepares the game for launch.

Meanwhile, Owlcat is making a substantially different RPG based around the popular Expanse license - a game that's much more closely inspired by Mass Effect. That project recently recruited the help of former Dragon Age writer David Gaider, and it will no doubt hope to fill a much-lamented hole created recently by the cancellation of Mass Effect 5.

The James Bond movies have been entertaining audiences for decades, with entire generations brought up on 007's adventures. Daniel Craig's Bond movies ended with No Time to Die, opening the door for a new actor to take on the mantle in the developing 26th movie by Denis Villeneuve. Fans have spent years taking bets on the next Bond, and the Oscar-nominated filmmaker recently trolled us at a recent event.

No Time to Die's ending shockingly killed off 007, a first for the long-running franchise (which is streaming with an Amazon Prime subscription). Those involved with the next movie have been keeping tight-lipped about casting, but Villeneuve spoke at the LACMA Art + Film Gala, where he spoke to the crowd and said:

With the blessing of my new friends at Amazon, I will reveal to you tonight who will be the next James Bond. The actor who will play the next James Bond is… And I will stop right now because Amy Pascal is about to have a heart attack.

What a tease. Clearly the acclaimed director knows that folks are dying to know who will take on the role of 007 in his James Bond movie. And what's a little light trolling among friends? Hopefully we'll get more answers about his developing blockbuster once Dune: Part Three hits theaters this December as half of Dunesday.

Denis Villeneuve's involvement in Bond 26 helping to buoy excitement for the mysterious project... even if we still don't know who will be playing the lead role. In a video from Variety's Instagram, he got honest about why he can't say much right now, offering:

I should not comment right now because every word I’m going to say is going to be scrutinized. I would just say that I’m having a great time.

The Arrival director was being cheeky at the event, but these comments show a much more sincere side of him. He's clearly thrilled to be behind the camera for the next James Bond movie, even if fans are desperate for any information regarding casting. You can see a video of him giving the above quote below:

It's been years since No Time to Die hit theaters back in 2021, fans have been curious about which actor will be passed the baton from Daniel Craig. Unfortunately we're still waiting on casting news, with fans tossing around a number of familiar names online. There are tons of rumors about who might be playing the martini-sipping agent, as well as chatter that the studio might go with an unknown rather than an established actor. Hopefully we get some answers soon.

All of the Bond movies are streaming on Amazon, and Denis Villeneuve's Dune: Part Three hits theaters December 18th as part of the 2026 movie release list. Fingers crossed that more Bond 26 info comes after that title gets its wide theatrical release.
