#3757. Overwatch doesn’t have ‘any intention’ of making 6-vs-6 the main mode, but it’s now ‘a second among equals’

The never-ending battle between Overwatch players choosing five-vs-five or six-vs-six will rage on.

In a new Director’s Take blog today, game director Aaron Keller confirmed that Overwatch will continue to support both formats, but with a renewed focus on the classic six-vs-six, which the studio is “starting to think of it as a second among equals.”

“We always say that we want to make the game you all want to play and it’s obvious that we have folks who want different things,” Keller said, citing player surveys that were very split between the two options, as seen above. “Over the past few years, we’ve realized that there doesn’t have to be a ‘winner’ between five-vs-five and six-vs-six. The real competition should be in your matches, not between two modes that can coexist. You can play either one (many people actually play both!) and we’re going to support that choice.”

Personally? I’m a fan of six-vs-six, but that’s because I’m a tank main. Solo tanking is a pain compared to having a buddy on the frontline with you, and I can see that there are many who agree with me…but also many who don’t. Overwatch will continue to feature both, Keller says, and there won’t be any radical switches soon either, other than an additional six-vs-six queue.

“Six-vs-six has been slowly growing in popularity over the last few years; however, the five-vs-five version of Open Queue was popular too,” Keller said. “We’d like to learn how many people are playing Open Queue six-vs-six for the role flexibility and how many people are playing it for the team size. Running both modes at the same time should produce some good data points to show us where we ought to be putting more energy.”

Keller warned that adding the new queue (Role Queue six-vs-six) instead of replacing an old one may impact queue times, but it “should be better overall for our community.” He also said that the team theorizes that some matchmaking changes coming in season six “will keep queue times more manageable” alongside the new option.

“We’ll put more energy into balance patches for [six-vs-six] and we’ll continue to look for the right format that really gives our community the experience they’re looking for,” Keller said. “Whether that’s Open Queue, Role Queue, a combination of both, or a new format that we’ve yet to try out, we’re here to figure out what works best for you.”

Those birds kept stealing all my good cards.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

What's worse than fighting one human-sized bird with sunglasses? Fighting two human-sized birds with sunglasses. That wasn't a usual problem in my everyday life until I started playing Stack Order's demo, the hand-drawn deckbuilder that's full of duels and fantastic combos.

The run began with my masked character locked away in a jail cell, not all that dissimilar to how I start most of my days. However, this time I was promptly freed by a stranger who wanted to help out. After handing me a deck of cards and talking me through how to use it, I was left to go on my merry way. The only problem was that I didn't get very far before a knight called Robert, who was very unhappy to see me out of my cell, butted in.

I've played my fair share of deckbuilders so it wasn't exactly a steep learning curve. But unlike some other games, Stack Order puts a very strong emphasis on stacking cards. You need to lose the bad habit of just playing one card at a time and instead start stacking cards at the first chance you get.

But, crucially, stacking cards doesn't necessarily mean you have to use them, you could get everything ready and then forfeit your go or just use a throwaway attack. Most killing blows in Stack Order come down all at once after you've stacked several cards all with varying multipliers and unleash it all at once.

Certain cards, for example, deal extra damage if they come before or after cards, others add damage to specific cards if they're stacked below them. You get a random assortment of cards on each turn, so you can't always bet on a dream stack, but if you're smart you can usually create one hell of a combo.

The only problem is that you're not the only one who can pack a punch. Each enemy I came up against had their own set of skills which changed the fight. Knight Robert had a simple yet effective attack / block combo, the Queen slowly poisoned me, but the birds, those two damn birds really topped it all.

First off there were two of them, which meant extra attacks, but to make matters worse each bird had a special effect that would see them deal extra damage the more cards you left on the table and would steal either the top of bottom card of each stack and use it to buff themselves, including how much they were able to heal. This made things really tricky.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

I quickly found out that if I didn't kill them quickly we'd roll into a painfully long stalemate, as I would just barely hang on with shields and they were able to heal 11 damage every third turn. Damage them enough and you can break some of their attacks, they'll still deal damage but won't get the bonus perk.

Managing how you build stacks, when you can't build multiple and also need to leave a sacrifice card for one of the birds to eat, is taxing to be sure. But that's what makes winning fights in Stack Order all the more rewarding.

I managed to experience this euphoria after I bested the pair of birds, but that wasn't the last I'd see of them as, after dying to the next boss, I had to restart my run. Soon I was fighting Robert, the Queen, and the dastardly bird duo all over again, and let me tell you it does not get easier the second time you fight them.

#3755. Hollow Knight Silksong physical editions mention multiple "free content packs" incoming, and call Sea of Sorrow a "giant expansion"

More than a year after its initial release, physical versions of Hollow Knight: Silksong are finally arriving on players' doorsteps. It's the same brilliant and sometimes thrillingly cruel Metroidvania Eurogamer gave five stars to, except this time a pack-in booklet seemingly reveals the existence of multiple "free content packs" alongside the Sea of Sorrow DLC.

Hollow Knight: Silksong's physical editions were originally set to be delivered from 10th November, but some early handovers have given us a peek inside the box. Redditor Me_975 posted pictures of their Nintendo Switch 2 Edition, and there's a few interesting tidbits tucked away - most notably in the manual's chapter on Content Packs.

"The world of Hollow Knight: Silksong will expand with free content packs," the booklet reads. "Prepare for even more adventures filled with new friends, new abilities, and new ferocious foes!"

Developer Team Cherry confirmed plans for post-launch Silksong support last year, but remained pretty tight-lipped about what exactly that would look like. The indie outfit then announced the nautically themed Sea of Sorrow expansion, though we now have proper confirmation there's more content packs still to come, which shouldn't be a huge shocker considering all the free post-launch love Hollow Knight (the first one) received.

Speaking of Sea of Sorrow, that's mentioned here too: "In the first giant expansion, voyage across and beneath a salt-stricken ocean brimming with mystery and menace."

Sea of Sorrow's original release window was a vague 2026 - time's a-ticking, Team Cherry. Still no release date so far, but the booklet does say it's "Coming Soon." Of course, Team Cherry are quite infamous for working on games until they balloon wildly out of control. After all, Silksong was once upon a time intended to be a Hollow Knight DLC, but with games this detailed, I can't really complain about waiting a little extra.

If you are interested in owning Silksong physically, it comes with a big map of Pharloom and the rest of the booklet also includes some really lovely art seemingly ripped straight from the game, as well.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I thought I'd seen most of the celebrity fashion from this year's LACMA Art+Film Gala, but apparently Emma Watson had other plans. The Harry Potter franchise star may be absent from the 2026 movie schedule, but she's certainly been making memorable Hollywood appearances lately. While everyone was busy admiring the outfits worn by Nicole Kidman, Kim Kardashian and the rest of the A-list guests, Watson attended without attracting nearly as much attention.

According to Los Angeles Magazine, Watson was among the guests celebrating filmmaker Denis Villeneuve and artist Vija Celmins. While other celebrities turned heads in elaborate LACMA outfits, Watson was noticeably absent from several prominent red-carpet fashion galleries. As you can see in the Instagram story she shared (see below), the Little Women actress was dressed like a fiery work of art.

Watson wore a striking, floor-length burgundy gown that looked as though someone had poured molten red glass over silk. The fitted, glossy bodice featured a rich crimson neckline and delicate straps draped across her shoulders, while the flowing skirt shimmered with deep red and wine-colored tones. It's a gorgeous look on its own, but the really fascinating part is how the material was created.

As Watson explained in her Instagram Stories, artist Caroline Zimbalist developed the fabric using a biopolymer-based material that's heated, mixed and poured by hand directly onto silk. Plant-derived glycerin gives the material its softness and flexibility, and as the water evaporates, it bonds with the silk to create that unusual, sculptural finish. So, yes, Watson essentially wore a piece of experimental textile art to an event celebrating art. I love this take on celebrity fashion.

Honestly, this is becoming something of a pattern for Watson. Back in September, the actress made another unexpected Hollywood appearance at the opening of the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, where she wore a gorgeous little black dress with an unconventional artistic twist. That one incorporated real flowers, carefully attached to a recycled velvet garment. Watson went viral for wearing the dress, as it looked like the flowers were floating across her body. The internet certainly had some fun with that one, especially Harry Potter fans. I have to admit, this latest look is maybe a bit more magical, and my favorite. The woman seems to appreciate a dress with a little more going on than meets the eye.

For that earlier appearance, Watson worked with stylist Jared Ellner and florist Anthony Maslo on a bespoke design featuring orchids, lilies and other blooms. In an interview with Vogue, she explained that the outfit celebrated the natural world and the beauty of things that don't last forever. Even the flowers were preserved afterward. I love that kind of attention to detail, especially when so many celebrity looks disappear into the endless stream of red carpet photographs.

LACMA seems like an especially fitting place for Watson to continue exploring the connection between clothing and artistic expression. The annual event brings together filmmakers, artists and fashion designers to support the museum's programming. This year's gathering, presented by Gucci and co-chaired by Leonardo DiCaprio and Eva Chow, raised nearly $7 million.

There was plenty of fashion to admire, too. Nicole Kidman wore an elaborate Chanel ensemble inspired by Edgar Degas' Little Dancer of Fourteen Years, while Anya Taylor-Joy turned heads in an archival Pierre Cardin design. The evening also featured a performance by Rosé, making it a pretty spectacular night even before I learned Watson was among the guests.

What I particularly love about Watson and her recent appearances is that she seems more interested in the creative work behind what she's wearing than making sure she gets captured on camera. She's also been an advocate for sustainable and ethical fashion for years, so seeing her embrace pieces with an artistic story behind them feels pretty fitting.

Of course, it's been quite some time since Watson appeared in a major movie. Her last feature was 2019's Little Women, and she's spoken candidly about why she stepped away from acting. She's since devoted much of her attention to other interests, including philanthropy and her Renais gin business.

That's two surprise appearances in Los Angeles this fall, both at events celebrating art and storytelling. If Watson keeps turning up in outfits with this much thought behind them, I may need to start paying closer attention to her Instagram Stories. Clearly, the usual red carpet galleries aren't telling me everything.

#3753. God of War: Ragnarok is reportedly the highest-earning PlayStation Studios game this generation, but Marvel's Spider-Man 2 isn't far behind

God of War: Ragnarok is the generation's best-selling and highest-earning PlayStation Studios game, according to a new report, but the full top 10 list has a few nice surprises.

In the four years since its PS5 release and two years since its PC port, God of War: Ragnarok has reportedly sold just over 20m copies and generated $1.4b in revenue, according to estimates from Alinea Analytics. About 27.5 percent of the 15m copies it sold on console came from physical editions, and the action blockbuster apparently sold a further 1.1m this year alone. Not bad, boy.

Those stats should bode well for the series' next romp God of War: Laufey - which sees Faye take the spotlight across a multi-mythological afterlife and was recently delayed into May 2027 - even if PlayStation moves away from PC ports for its signature single-player games.

Kratos and Atreus only narrowly beat out perhaps the biggest superhero of them all: Marvel's Spider-Man 2, a game that reportedly made a whopping $1.3b off 19.1m copies across PS5 and PC. The Spidey sequel should keep swinging even higher as the years chug on, though - the report states that sales always surge during the holiday months, and this year's big screen behemoth Spider-Man: Brand New Day led to an even bigger spike than usual.

Racing sim royalty Gran Turismo 7 ($841m), bug-squashing phenomenon Helldivers 2 ($786m), robo-dino sequel Horizon: Forbidden West ($485m), vengeful spirit sim Ghost of Yotei ($410m), undead remake The Last of Us Part 1 ($341m), multidimensional romp Ratchet and Clank: Rift Apart ($334m), Stellar Blade ($316m) and delightful throwback Astro Bot ($292m) round out the top 10 games published by PlayStation Studios this generation.

It's worth noting that Helldivers 2 and Stellar Blade were developed by studios outside the PlayStation umbrella, but the console maker still published both upon release. Ghost of Yotei's performance is also particularly impressive since Sucker Punch's sequel has only been out for a year and didn't get the benefit of a PC port, like many of its PS5 siblings. The success couldn't save Sucker Punch from recent layoffs, however.

On PlayStation's decision to kill disc-based physical releases, analyst Rhys Elliott said that the bottom five games in the list together made $281.7m this year alone: "PlayStation wants those numbers to be bigger in the coming years, which is one of the reasons it's killing the disc (alongside the better margins it and publishers get through digital.)"

When it comes to monitors, Alienware increasingly has a habit of undercutting the competition. The new Alienware AW3226Q is no exception, offering LG's stunning new 4K RGB-stripe Tandem OLED panel for by far the lowest price yet.

PC Gamer's got your back Our experienced team dedicates many hours to every review, to really get to the heart of what matters most to you. Find out more about how we evaluate games and hardware.

You know Alienware's 5K2K 39-inch ultrawide OLED gaming monitor beast, the AW3926QW, the one I reviewed the other day? It's an absolute beauty, probably my favourite current PC monitor, save for one niggly flaw. But what if you fancy something similar, but cheaper and in a more conventional 32-inch 4K form factor? Well, give it up for the new Alienware AW3226Q, because it ticks all those boxes.

Notably, it sports exactly the same LG Tandem WOLED panel tech as its bigger 39-inch sibling. That includes being the latest RGB-stripe variant of that new LG OLED panel generation that everyone is going bananas for.

Well, it's nearly the same. For reasons that aren't entirely clear, this 32-inch 4K panel clocks in at 250 nits full-screen brightness and 1,000 nits peak HDR. The aforementioned 39 incher rocks 300 nits and 1,300 nits figures for the same metrics, respectively.

250 nits full screen, 1,000 nits peak HDR

LG Tandem WOLED RGB-stripe panel, 2x HDMI 2.1, DisplayPort 1.4, USB-A/C hub, 3.5mm audio

✅ You're an OLED purist: LG's new RGB-stripe WOLED tech offers beautifully neutral colours.

❌ You want the brightest possible OLED experience: This version of LG's Tandem WOLED panel technology takes a small brightness hit.

As it happens, the numbers for this 32-inch 4K model are actually more in line with expectations for this panel type. The thing is, with all previous WOLED panel generations, LG used a white subpixel to boost brightness.

This new pure RGB-stripe—or red, green, blue—item ditches the white subpixel in favour of pixel precision and improved colour volume. But that comes with a cost in terms of peak brightness.

Even the 39-inch AW3926QW is a little dimmer than the RGWB version of LG's latest Tandem OLED monitor panel tech, where the "W" in "RGWB" indicates the added white subpixel. Oh, and just for clarity, the "W" in "WOLED" has always referred to the white colour of the light produced by the emissive OLED material in all of the subpixels, rather than the added white subpixels in all previous WOLED monitor generations prior to the newest RGB-stripe variants. Baffling, but there you go.

Anywho, monitors with RGWB Tandem OLED panels, including the Asus ROG Strix XG32UQWMS I reviewed recently, tend to weigh in around 330 nits full-screen and 1,500 nits peak HDR. So the 39-inch 5K2K RGB-stripe panel gives less away in terms of brightness than expected, and in turn this new 32-inch 4K model is pretty much where you'd expect it to be.

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

Got all that? Then it's also worth understanding that those brightness figures can be misleading. Like I said, LG has been including a fourth white subpixel in all of its previous WOLED monitor panel generations to boost brightness. But that doesn't automatically boost colour brightness. At least it can't while maintaining colour volume.

That's why Samsung's competing QD-OLED panels, as also used by a wide variety of monitor makers including Alienware, have often looked more vibrant despite typically offering slightly lower ratings. Samsung has never used an additional white subpixel, so its brightness rating reflects real-world usage. And real-world gaming means a colour image rather than a pure white image pretty much all the time.

The point I'm making here is that it's important not to assume that the 4K RGB-stripe Tandem WOLED panel in this new Alienware is a step backwards just because it has lower brightness ratings than RGWB Tandem WOLED in monitors like that Asus model I mentioned above. It's more complicated than that.

Along with the brightness and colour volume implications, the RGB-stripe has the same pixel precision and text quality upsides here as it does on other RGB-stripe OLEDs. In short, the Windows OS assumes it is rendering to a conventional RGB-stripe subpixel layout, so having RGB-stripe solves issues like fuzzy text and colour fringing.

It's important not to assume that the 4K RGB-stripe Tandem WOLED panel in this new Alienware is a step backwards just because it has lower brightness ratings.

As for the rest of the speeds and feeds, well, the refresh is a relatively modest 165 Hz, the panel is flat, and it's covered in a glossy glare coating. Inputs include DisplayPort 1.4 and two HDMI 2.1 ports, but there's no USB-C for single-cable connectivity, albeit along with the two USB-A data ports, there is a USB–C downstream socket as part of the USB hub.

Oh, and I haven't mentioned the price. It's $699 or £649 at launch, which is pretty punchy, especially given the cutting-edge panel tech. Heck, the 34-inch ultrawide AW3426DW is more expensive. It's also not far off half the price of the Asus ROG Swift PG32UCWM, which has the same RGB-stripe panel, albeit running at a higher refresh and with more features.

So, the surprisingly low price perhaps explains the 165 Hz as opposed to 240 Hz refresh and lack of USB-C support. It's probably also why there's no dual-mode support offering a higher refresh rate at a lower resolution.

If that's the stats and specs covered, what's the actual gaming experience like? Mostly pretty fantastic. Like the bigger AW3926QW, I really like the AW3226Q's overall look and colour balance. It fixes the slightly washed out and green-tinted vibe of LG's RGWB panels without suffering from the overly warm colour temperature and purple-tint in bright ambient light of competing Samsung QD-OLED-based monitors.

In many ways, this is the perfect OLED panel tech, it's just so nice. The colours look super natural, the lighting control is perfect, and the response is basically instant. The 4K resolution on a 32-inch panel also makes for razor-sharp detail. It's pretty much the definitive modern PC gaming experience.

OKay, the 165 Hz refresh is a touch pedestrian these days, but this isn't an esports model and it's definitely a compromise built out of chasing affordability. And even with an RTX 5090, you're not going to be playing many modern games at 4K at 200fps-plus, in reality.

It's pretty much the definitive modern PC gaming experience.

The arguable exception to all that is full-screen brightness, which is just a touch disappointing. A lot of the time you won't notice it. On the Windows desktop if you enable dark mode and you haven't got a very bright browser or app window open, this monitor looks really punchy and vibrant.

The same goes for most game scenes with HDR enabled. They look absolutely stellar, with both bright and dark image elements precisely controlled in the same image. That's OLED per-pixel lighting for you, there's nothing quite like it. As ever, of course, the sizzle of small HDR highlights like light sources, sparks and explosions are a sight to behold.

Where this RGB-stripe 32 incher isn't quite so impressive is brighter outdoor game scenes. Here, it can look just a bit dull, with that 250 nit full-screen capability holding it back. To an extent, the 39-inch 5K2K model has the same problem. But it's that little bit brighter. We're talking fine margins, but where the 39 incher mostly seems to be just punchy enough, this 32-inch sibling just falls short of being enjoyably vibrant that little bit more often.

That said, Alienware has included a range of HDR modes, including standard HDR 400 and HDR 1000 models, plus an HDR 1000 Bright mode. The latter is supposed to offer the best of the other two modes in a single setting and from a subjective experience perspective, it largely does just that, offering the best this panel can achieve in terms of both full-screen brightness and peak HDR performance for small, super-bright highlights.

I'm pretty confident you can consider vignette dimming a solved problem.

So, what about that niggle I mentioned up front? With the 39-inch Alienware AW3926QW, I was disappointed to confirm that community reports of so-called "vignette dimming" were accurate. Long story short, Alienware had implemented an OLED protection feature known as CPC or Convex Power Control that slightly dims the edge of the panel when gameplay is detected.

The idea is to prevent static game interface elements like mini maps or health bars from causing burn-in. The problem was that Alienware didn't provide a toggle for CPC. It was always enabled. And all of that is also true for the new 32-inch Alienware AW3226Q.

At least it was. On November 5th, Alienware released a new firmware update for the 39-inch Alienware AW3926QW which includes a toggle for CPC, though it's called "Edge-Dimming" in the OSD. I haven't tested it myself, but it's reported to remove the vignette dimming when disabled. Hurrah.

Just a day later, Alienware released a similar update for this 32 incher. Unfortunately, we just missed the update before our review sample had to be returned. But I'm pretty confident you can consider vignette dimming a solved problem.

And in case you are wondering, while the updated OSD menu does warn you that edge-dimming "is a feature to improve OLED panel durability", Dell has not said that disabling it voids the three-year warranty, which could have been a worry.

So, yeah, I like the Alienware AW3226Q. I like it a lot. Alienware has specced it cleverly to hit a surprisingly appealing price point. It's not a budget option, obviously. But for an RGB-stripe 4K 32-inch OLED, it's got to be a bit of a bargain. The really tough question is whether I'd go for this or one of the OG 32-inch 4K models based on Samsung's first stab at a QD-OLED panel in that format. You can often grab such monitors, such as the MSI MAG 321UP for even less money. That's a very tough call.

I'm Commander Shepard and this is my favorite video on the internet.

This N7 Day was the first without developer BioWare around, but fans of the Mass Effect series didn't let 7th November go by quietly. The community managed to get several notable Mass Effect actors to lend their voice to the increasingly loud 'SaveMassEffect' movement.

In the weeks since BioWare's shock closure and Mass Effect Universe's cancellation, the community-organised We Are Mass Effect group have put up billboards in Times Square, a mobile billboard outside BioWare Edmonton's former office and much more while directing attention to an online petition.

Today is a very special day for Mass Effect fans. We've worked incredibly hard to bring together most of the original Mass Effect trilogy's voice cast to share a very important message with you. We need to #SaveMassEffect. https://t.co/FOp0qp4wBI

And for the series' annual celebration, the group managed to get a sizable portion of the Mass Effect cast to join in. Commander Shepard actors Jennifer Hale and Mark Meer, original trilogy composer Sam Hulick, Garrus' Brandon Keener, Jack's Courtnay Taylor, Tali'Zorah's Ash Sroka, Thane's Keythe Farley and many more all showed up in a two-minute video to help potentially salvage the series - sometimes in character.

"When we heard about the formal closing of Boware, I felt weirdly hopeful," Hale said in a separate interview with IGN. "I can't explain it. I just got so weirdly hopeful. #3748. How to change layers in WoW Forever? (After the layer size change)

If you want to play with friends in WoW: Forever, you have to go back to one of WoW's most dreaded concepts - layers and shards.

World of Warcraft: Forever skips realms and introduces gameplay rulesets instead, where you can pick your preferred playstyle and get whisked to an Azeroth populated with like-minded individuals. But things can get complicated if, say, you want to play with your friends or guildmates from across the world.

Plus, it’s not like Blizzard will squeeze everyone using your gameplay ruleset into the same world instance. This is where layers come in, and it’s similar to, but also very different from, its original iteration in Classic.

Others new to WoW might be wondering what exactly layers are, and how they might affect their WoW: Forever experience.

So we know MMOs have servers, and each WoW server has a realm that contains a version of Azeroth and the players inside it. Of course, we can’t expect Blizzard to spawn everyone at once, since we’d overcrowd the game world and break the experience.

When a location gets a high-enough population, WoW uses sharding to copy the area into a “shard” and transfers some players there. A shard is a perfectly working copy of a location, complete with NPCs and objects, except you can only see and interact with players of the same shard.

The idea is to manage overpopulation by keeping player counts at a certain number. This keeps lag manageable and ensures there are enough mobs and quest items for everyone in any given zone.

Since shards are zone-wide, you can see players “disappear” into a new zone because they’re crossing over to a new shard (called phasing). If you’re approaching a zone where all shards are at capacity, you’d hit a soft “loading” queue before you enter. Worst case, you get disconnected from the server, which can ruin your momentum.

WoW Retail still uses sharding. It sometimes implements cross-realm zones (CRZs), so low-population realms can share low-population zones.

We got to layering at the launch of WoW Classic in 2019, where it was presented as a bigger solution to server population. Sharding at the time just didn’t feel like a practical choice, as they’d have to create hundreds of shards per zone.

“We had some serious concerns about what would happen when realms started to mature, and populations shifted,” Blizzard noted about sharding in the release of Battle for Wintergrasp in Wrath Classic. “Would we have hundreds of realms with low populations a few months in?”

So they came up with layers, which is sharding but applied to the whole game world. Upon meeting specific population conditions, Blizzard can create a copy of Azeroth and transfer players there.

But it’s not a perfect solution. Too much layering could result in dead cities, and too little overcrowds areas. It can hurt the economy as well, as you can layer-hop to get more resources from another layer once your layer’s route runs out.

Classic moved away from layering just a few months in November 2019 and converged everyone into a single layer.

Read what’s behind the latest news in gaming (with a bit of snark) by subscribing to the Destructoid Checkpoint newsletter!

Players reintroduced the layering and sharding discourse back into Forever overpopulation concerns during launch. We don’t have the full picture of how Blizzard is managing Forever servers as of writing, but players seem to have noticed enough to make informed assumptions:

Instead of realms, we choose a ruleset that represents our preferred playstyle and play with others who choose the same. In theory, it’s a “realmless” system, and our ruleset of choice is functionally a mega server that our fellow ruleset comrades share.

Forever seems to have retained the Retail sharding system. But this time, there’s a chance you can auto-switch layers during the transition. This seems to have carried over from beta. Redditor u/Kellian noted that per-zone “loading” means hostiles and friendlies phase in and out, and can even stop PvP.

Building upon the ruleset is what Blizzard called the familiar faces system. As explained in their BlizzCon 2026 deep-dive, this will have players more consistently encounter the same strangers throughout their leveling journey. The goal is for these familiar faces to give Forever a stronger sense of community spirit, and may even encourage teaming up while you level. This also extends to guilds, so they can potentially pull you into their layers.

At random intervals during your sessions (sometimes none at all), you might encounter a prompt that warns you of a World Refresh. Either you do the refresh now or wait a couple of minutes. This isn’t any cause for alarm, as it just means the game will transfer you to a new instance or layer.

These refreshes often happen to balance the current population. You remain in the same spot, but your immediate surroundings might be different, like there might be more players, more mobs, or both.

Switching between layers in Forever can be done in a variety of ways, but there’s no manual options button to do so. Instead, you can do some things to “force” your way into a layer switch. Popular methods you can try include:

At launch, game dev Aggrend said they would look into how players lamented how sparsely populated the game world felt. A few days later, some players noticed so many characters for so few mobs.

This was especially challenging in PvP, where one faction can dominate a layer and make it difficult for the opposing one to level up or gather resources.

Redditor u/sknilegap doesn’t even call it layering at all, but actually just sharding. And their problem has less to do with the technology itself, but more with its impact on the experience at large.

“I am fine with the necessity of the system. Just keep it immersive,” they said in their post. “Make me sticky to those crossing over around the same time window as me. So […] we all see each other on the other side of the next zone, grouped or not.”

You can play World of Warcraft: Forever on PC and macOS.

#3747. Nintendo Switch Players Will Soon Be Able To Gift Digital Games, Kinda

A new Switch system update later this month is finally bringing us the ability to gift games via the Nintendo eShop, albeit with some hefty restrictions.

Digital games are increasingly becoming the norm across the games industry, yet strangely the concept of gifting digital games has yet to be widely adopted across all storefronts. While Steam and many PC platforms have supported the ability to send digital games to friends for at least a decade, on console only Microsoft allows Xbox players to do the same. Without it, people have simply had to make do with digital store cards. For Nintendo platforms, however, the company are promising to slightly change that and allow directly gifting games, âjust in time for the holidays.â

The feature, added in firmware update 23.5.0 and launching November 16, will allow players within a family group on Nintendo Switch to gift digital games to one another via the eShop. Once the feature has been activated, players will need to navigate to a gameâs store page where a check box will allow us to give the game as a gift. After checkout, you’ll select the player within your “family” to give the game, select from eight colors of digital wrapping paper, and the game will appear on their system.

There are notable limitations to this new feature. Supervised accounts within a family group are unable to gift games, and the number of games able to be purchased and gifted within an unspecified period is limited. Some games may also be unavailable for gifting, and any games gifted are immediately sent to the receiving player (so donât go buying those Christmas gifts early!). The feature, however, will be available to players both on the original Nintendo Switch as well as the Switch 2.

Itâs a welcome addition, though the inability to freely gift a game to anyone on your friends list (as seen on Steam) makes the feature bizarrely limited. Still, the fact its available at all is welcome for parents of gaming kids, or the found family of friends sharing a Nintendo Switch Online Family Plan.

The late Patrick Stewart was a celebrated dramatist, but he also had great comedic chops. It's something I don't think about often, until I saw that he wrote his own eulogy over a decade ago, and it's so hilarious.

For fans who need a break from the heartfelt tributes and touching stories, I implore you to check out his performance done for a Just for Laughs gala in 2015. Stewart took the stage to perform his own eulogy, but considering this was a comedy event, he had a twist in store for Trekkies:

Sir Patrick Stewart was more than just an actor, he was the greatest actor ever. He was also a husband, a father, and a friend. But most of all, he was an objectophile who achieved sexual congress with thousands of inanimate objects.

The audience burst into laughter because what else can you do at the end of that statement? Here's the guy who played one of the best Star Trek characters of all time, claiming he's having sex with furniture and other things.

It's something I'd never seen until after his passing, and I'm glad. All the sadness I had reading tributes and stories about his life is off to the side right now, as I listened to Stewart continue his hilarious bit:

As a boy, Sir Patrick entertained his classmates at Mirfield Secondary Modern School where he dutifully honed his craft as an actor, developing his now signature baritone voice and made sweet, secret lunch hour love to the janitor’s floor polishing machine.

It's one of those jokes that works really well because of who the one telling it is. So many co-stars have come through the woodwork in recent weeks talking about how sweet he was, and how humble an actor he was despite his fame. To think he'd have some odd, deviant behavior lurking beneath the surface as bizarre as this would be horrifying, and makes it so funny.

It's a funny eulogy, but it only worked in full if he was able to "land the plane" in terms of bringing it full circle. Fortunately the actor had the ultimate closer, revealing to the howling audience that they were sitting in chairs that he had defiled just minutes before their arrival:

In addition to winning the audience over with his wit, warmth, and humanity, Patrick also realized his final wish. Mere seconds before you, the audience entered, he rubbed his unwashed genitals on each and every seat of Montreal's Place Des Arts! Sir Patrick Stewart, you will be missed.

Many people will remember Patrick Stewart for Star Trek and X-Men, and rightfully so. That doesn't mean he didn't have memorable comedy roles, however, such as when he played King Richard in Robin Hood: Men in Tights. He also received an Emmy nomination for a guest role in Frasier, and he had a great night hosting Saturday Night Live.

There's a part of me sad that Patrick Stewart essentially worked up until his death, but also so grateful that he's left behind such a body of work to sift through. I still love hearing the touching stories and tributes about his life, but it's good to know I have this hilarious eulogy to look back on in the coming days to break up the sad moments.

CinemaBlend continues to offer condolences to the family and friends of Patrick Stewart. He made us laugh and cry, and it's nice to see evidence of that on the internet for all to see and enjoy.

#3745. GTA 6 pre-orders are tracking "well above expectations" and the game will "set a new baseline" for Take-Two, says CEO Strauss Zelnick

Today, as part of Take-Two Interactive Software's Q2 2027 earnings call, Strauss Zelnick noted that pre-orders for Grand Theft Auto 6 are tracking "far above expectations", and is certain that soon "numbers will speak for themselves" when it comes to the game.

Zelnick also promised GTA Online and GTA 5 will continue to receive updates in order to support the "nearly 235 million" units sold to date across "an unprecedented three console generations". The GTA series as a whole has, to date, sold over 480 million units. Karl Statoff, president at Take-Two, adds the launch of GTA 6 will be a "defining moment for the company and global entertainment industry". Zelnick adds, later in a question and answer session, that he expects GTA 6 to "set a new baseline" for Take-Two. "The future's really bright across the board," he notes.

For the next quarter, Take-Two expects to deliver $3.35 billion to $3.5 billion - with "recurrent consumer spending" to raise by 12 percent, driven by "the groundbreaking release" of Grand Theft Auto 6, and expects to see "significant growth for the Grand Theft Auto series", driven by sales of - specifically - Grand Theft Auto 6's Ultimate Edition, which includes add-on content, and that most people are pre-ordering at its $100 price point. That bonus $20 between the $80 base edition and the Ultimate Edition is counted as "recurrent consumer spending", as is part of that massive bump the company has seen.

It also seems that we will see more GTA games - or content, at least - sooner than expected. "We do think that the nature and velocity of the content we'll see from our iconic franchises, including GTA, will look dramatically different over the next decade." It's a vague comment, but assumedly the work done on the engine and backend of GTA 6 means we'll see more content arriving in shorter order than we're used to for the series. This is per an article published by IGN in line with the earning's call going live.

Elsewhere in the earnings call, Take-Two referred to its current setup with its mobile, sports, 'core new IP' and 'core existing IP' as "the strongest development pipeline in the company's history". In terms of new IP, Zelnick directed investors to consider the launches of incoming projects like Ken Levine's mysterious Judas and Project Ethos (which we don't know too much about yet, other than it's billed as a "roguelike hero shooter"). For core IP, 8 sequels and 7 remakes, remasters, and platform extensions.

Buoyed by these plans, Zelnick outlines that he believes that fiscal year 2027 "will be a historic year for Take-Two" as the company is buoyed by "recent and upcoming releases". No prizes for what that's referring to. If you're curious about what sort of numbers we may be looking at here, all you need to do is cast your mind back to 2014, where you will remember GTA 5 made $1bn in just three days.

DLSS 5 has been out for a while now, love it or hate it, but obviously not for AMD cards. Well, not officially, anyway. We have previously seen and tried mods that get the machine learning-aided neural rendering tech up and running using AMD RX 9000-series silicon, and now it looks like there's a significantly improved one.

AMDLSS5 version 2.0 is now out (via Wccftech), and it's claiming some impressive improvements compared to other DLSS 5 mods. Specifically, compared with "other mods", it's claiming +64% fps in Resident Evil Requiem, and +11% fps compared with the previous version of this one.

That's particularly great, if true, because our Dave's testing of DLSS 5 on an AMD Radeon RX 9070 XT using a different mod was, erm, not pretty. We're talking just 9 fps in Cyberpunk 2077, admittedly at 4K res on RT Ultra settings, but that was with FSR 4 on and set to Balanced.

It's not all the mod's fault, though, as DLSS 5 itself can be very intensive to run, even on an Nvidia GPU. Our Andy found this out when he tried running it in NBA 2K27. Frame rates there dropped up to 73% at 4K while using an RTX 5080, and there were significant drops at lower resolutions, too.

It's worth noting that some of the Reddit comments say the quality isn't very good with the mod enabled. That's to be expected, I suppose, for something unofficial, but it's just something to keep in mind if you're planning on installing it.

Installation itself involves simply downloading the files and running the installer. It then "installs, updates or removes the mod with one click."

#3742. Valve Is Improving The Data About How Well A Game Will Run On Your Steam Deck

Steam has delivered a refresh of its store page for Steam Deck owners, allowing people to see the average framerate a game will run at on the handheld device based on the performance data of other players.

While games often arrive as verified to work on Steam Deck, this doesn’t always translate to workingÂ well. To let players know just how well a game will perform on Valve’s portable PC, others who have opted in to share their data will contribute to a consensus on possible framerates.

Under the additional info for Steam Deck compatibility on the game page, a new note will display the average framerate. It will also be possible to expand this data further by looking at the histogram, which will qualify the average into a graph that not only displays how common it is for a game to run at that framerate, but also how often the game hitches or stutters for players.

According to Valve, although the current information relies on standardized test criteria, the denominations âmay not match every customerâs bar for acceptable gameplay.â The company is also planning to expand this feature beyond Steam Deck in order to provide framerate information for more devices. The feature is already live for games with enough data points to provide an average. For example, right now Final Fantasy VII Rebirth shows that Steam Deck OLED players run the game at an average of 37 frames per second, while those playing Hades II are seeing 88 FPS on the same hardware.

With portable PC devices like Steam Deck, ROG Ally and even the Ayn Thor becoming more standard for players who donât need the most expensive hardware, seeing how a game will perform with more specificity is only a good thing. It doesnât hurt that Steam are planning to expand the Steam Deck lineup in future, and having such features available only makes the hardware more accessible for those less accustomed to PC gaming.

#3741. As investors ask about GTA 6 and AI, Take-Two CEO once again puts faith in dev creativity, states making hit games "remains the purview of human beings"

"Making a big hit was hard then, and it's hard now, and it's going to be hard in the future."

Today, as part of Take-Two Interactive Software's Q2 2027 earnings call, Strauss Zelnick fielded questions from investors after presenting the financial results of the company. One caller was concerned about AI - specifically about the proliferation of AI-powered compilations and decompilations that have been raising piracy concerns for publishers over the past few weeks.

Zelnick notes that "[the video games] business has been largely immune to piracy" thanks to factors like file size, how console ecosystems work, and aspects related to the online nature of the games industry. That said, Strauss continues, there is a threat posed to the industry because of AI. However, he assures listening investors that Take-Two is appropriately scaling its measures against bad faith actors using artificial intelligence.

"We are utterly focused on enhancing our technical defences and enhancing our legal activities appropriately. And - at the same time, without in any way being cavalier - every entertainment business that exists is subject to some element of piracy, [and] this is likely to invade our business to a greater or lesser extent. I think it will be manageable and we are focused on it."

Zelnick pivots back to AI again later in the call, where one investor once again asks about AI, seemingly keen to learn whether the CEO feels it can provide GTA 6 developer Rockstar with any kind of "competitive advantage" in the games industry. Given Zelnick's previous comments on the subject, his answer was not a complete surprise.

"It's always been true [that technology benefits us]," explains Zelnick. "We've always created our entertainment inside computers with technology. All advances have benefited us, and I don't expect that that will change - in fact, I hope it'll accelerate. I think at the same time, what we're known for [at Take-Two] is the desire to make the best entertainment on Earth. And, more often than not, we have succeeded - and the creativity that drives that success is human creativity harnessing technology. And I think that's what you'll see in the future, too.

"Undoubtedly some of the most recent technological advances that you've seen have made it easier to create assets. Where all that is consistent with the story of our business. When I started in interactive entertainment (longer ago than I would like to say), it was really difficult to create an asset in a computer. Today, it's a whole lot easier - but you know what's not easier? Making a big hit. Making a big hit was hard then, and it's hard now, and it's going to be hard in the future. And hit creation remains the purview of human beings."

This isn't the first instance of AI skepticism we've seen from Strauss Zelnick. Back in March, he outright rejected the idea that AI can tackle games on the scale of GTA 6. Elsewhere in the call, the Take-Two CEO reiterated how well GTA 6 is tracking as he reasserted pre-order numbers are well above expectations, and promised that the success of the game will "set a new baseline" for Take-Two's gaming business.

Presley Gerber tragically passed away after working toward addiction recovery in September of this year. He left behind his famous parents, Cindy Crawford and Casamigos businessman Rande Gerber, and his sister Kaia, who have all been reeling in the wake of his death. This week, the Bottoms cast member addressed that grief head on with a viral post about grief “coming in waves.”

It’s from The Year of Magical Thinking by Joan Didion, a book with a lighthearted title that betrays its heavy subject material and that I still think about to this day. It helped me get through my mother’s battle with cancer, and I think it’s a helpful read for anyone going through it with a loved one. However, it particularly highlights grief in the face of addiction, and I would guess was especially pertinent to Gerber.

Kaia shared a post this week about the titles on grief that have been helpful after losing her brother. A separate slide included a quote from Didion that's one of the more memorable from the book.

Grief, when it comes, is nothing we expect it to be. Grief has no distance. Grief, comes in waves, paroxysms, sudden apprehensions that weaken the knees and blind the eyes and obliterate the dailiness of life.

Here's what else she's been reading in recent days, per her post.

A post shared by Library Science (@libraryscience)

Didion wrote The Year of Magical Thinking in 2005, while frequenting hospitals as her daughter Quintana Roo dealt with health issues. All of this came just shortly after losing her husband, beloved author John Gregory Dunne. The book follows Didion’s experience with grief following her husband’s death alongside her daughter’s hospitalizations and complications related to alcohol abuse. The book ends without us knowing what was next for Quintana Roo and Didion, though her daughter would pass away in August of 2005, just shortly before the author would publish the book.

Joan Didion mixes up stories about experiences she'd shared with her family over time with prose about everything she was also going through in the moment. It’s beautiful, direct, and devastating writing. I wouldn’t recommend picking it up as a beach read, but if you are going through something in your family, it’s helpful for contextualizing feelings and realizing humans are similar. We all go through the pain and anger and feelings of helplessness when we are losing a loved one.

It's not one of the author's titles that have yet made it to the big screen, but Didion’s book is powerful. I read almost 10 years ago and some of her words are still with me. It holds up years after it was published, and it’s a gripping read. I’m glad Kaia Gerber found solace in it. I hope her parents, and celebrity pals like George and Amal Clooney, have found some solace too.

#3738. Switch 2 and Switch consoles updated to version 23.5.0 as Nintendo quietly re-introduces eShop gifting

Nintendo has just pushed out a new update to all Switch and Switch 2 consoles, bringing the firmware on both up to version 23.5.0. The headline change with the new update is support and compatibility for an upcoming update that will allow members of a Nintendo Account family group to gift games to one another.

The feature itself is expected to go live on 17th November, 2026. "Just in time for the holidays, a new feature will let family group members gift digital games to other members of their group," says a post on a dedicated blog on the Nintendo site. "You will be able to gift digital products that you purchase through Nintendo eShop on your device to family group members. This includes eligible games as well as DLC and upgrade packs. As a reminder, anyone with a Nintendo Account can easily set up a family group and add members (up to 8 total)."

The publisher notes, however, that "some products may not be eligible for digital gifting" and that "supervised accounts are not able to send digital gifts". Additionally, "the number of digital gift purchases allowed in a given period is limited".

"This feature is a great way to celebrate a special occasion with your kids. Happy gifting!" concludes Nintendo. Just in time for the holidays, how thoughtful. It's worth noting that a previous iteration of this support was included back on the Nintendo Wii, but that was much more robust than this - back then, the publisher allowed users to send WiiWare or Virtual Console games to anyone on their Wii Friend list via the Wii Shop Channel, rather than just those limited to their immediate group. This functionality was lost in 2019, alongside the closure of the Wii Shop Channel.

#3737. Nintendo Shuts Down Switch 2 Jailbreak, Sending Hackers Back To Square One

On October 22, news broke that the Switch 2 had been jailbroken for the first time. This meant that it wasâkindaâpossible to mod and dump games on the machine, which in the past would have opened the floodgates to third-party operating systems being installed and an accessible piracy scene. But not this time. Due to the incredibly complicated nature of the jailbreak, the need for now-delisted sofrware SmileBASIC, and that it was software based rather than hardware, Nintendo has been able to shut it down with its latest firmware update.

In the past, Nintendo’s portable consoles have become enormously popular among homebrew developers and the piracy scene for the ease with which they could be adapted. The Nintendo DS (its most successful console until the Switch, selling 154 million units and just shy of a billion games) had the infamous R4 cart onto which ROMs could be installed, while the original model of the Nintendo Switch (157 million units, 1.6 billion games) could be jailbroken due to a hardware issue that Nintendo couldn’t patch out. These exploits didn’t appear to hinder the consoles’ successes, but Nintendo remains resolute in its fury against such actions.

By October 26, hackers had figured out how to get more out of the Switch 2’s very limited exploit, able to dump games as ROMs and dig into the console’s file systems, which would usually be the beginning of emulation plans and homebrew development. Now, however, as reported by Oatmeal Dome, all this is patched out by the device’s 23.5.0 firmware update.

The OS exploit used in the recent jailbreak has been patched in version 23.5.0.

Dumping and modding games will be impossible again from this point forward, with the exception of some cartridge games (and maybe game updates) that are released in the near future.

— OatmealDome (@OatmealDome) November 10, 2026

This is possible because the issues discovered were software based, rather than something intrinsic to the physical hardware inside the Switch 2, as had been the case for the original model of the Switch 1. There, Nintendo had to change the manufacturing, and there was little that could be done to stop Switch 1 users from taking advantage, so long as they didn’t log in to Nintendo’s online services. Of course, of the tens of millions of people who owned the Switch that could do it, vanishingly few actually did, and software sales broke all of Nintendo’s records.

Eventually the crackers will find a way, because eventually they always do, but in this case it could be many years away.

The Australian STEM Videogame Challenge, a "free national videogame development competition for students," has confirmed that the rise of generative AI means this year's event will be the last.

The end of the STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) Videogame Challenge was first reported on Reddit last week, when someone claiming to be a judge in the program said they'd received an email informing them that "after 12 wonderful years," the 2026 event would mark its end.

Speculation as to the cause of the program's cancellation focused primarily on the presence of AI in entries: Another self-proclaimed judge said the problem wasn't merely the use of AI in itself but that "some students just completely generate their games with AI."

"How do you mark that? You can't just give them a zero," the judge wrote. "It's so hard to tell what was or wasn't generated using AI, and especially hard since that's the way the industry is going."

That same person also suggested, however, that funding cutbacks could have been an even bigger factor in the decision, saying that "projects like this are the first to get cut" when government budgets get tight.

Now the Australian Council for Educational Research has confirmed that the cancellation was in fact due to AI.

"After more than a decade inspiring the next generation of young creators, the current 2026 Australian STEM Video Game Challenge will be the competition's final chapter," Cathy Zemaitis, Head of the Student Learning and Progress division at ACER, told PC Gamer.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

"The decision was driven by the rapid and complex rise of generative AI in game development, making it harder to judge what students made themselves, and moving the program away from its original purpose."

So, that's that: A program aimed at encouraging kids to learn has come to an end because the kids learned how to get around the learning part. It's sad, although as a former high school reprobate myself I can't be too critical of the young'uns for doing what they do. I do wonder, though, what all of this might say about our future: Where will we be when we know how to prompt, but not how to create?

Zemaitis added that organizers are not looking at ways to adjust the program to accommodate generative AI: "There are no plans to pursue alternative options for delivering the Australian STEM Videogame Challenge, however we're always looking for how we can partner with schools and the sector more broadly to deliver programs that enrich the learning experience of students." She also encouraged educators looking for other ways to "keep students challenged" to check out the International Mathematical Modelling Challenge.

Minor spoilers ahead for Episode 2 of The Gilded Age Season 4.

Shortly after its debut, Julian Fellowes' The Gilded Age joined the ranks of HBO shows that got the world talking. Fans of Downton Abbey were thrilled at the new series set in America (streaming with a HBO Max subscription), and we're two episodes into its fourth season on the air. The show is full of Broadway royalty, and two more stars of the Great White Way have just joined the fun. So what is it going to take to get a full-blown musical episode?

The Gilded Age Season 4 started off with a bang, with fans concerned about Marian and Larry's relationship after their tryst. The Gilded Age cast is obviously full of Broadway icons, such as Audra McDonald, Kelli O'Hara, Denée Benton, Donna Murphy, and Celia Keenan-Bolger. Now we've got two more with Bonnie Milligan and Taylor Trensch joining the fun in the new season.

Milligan plays Mrs. Louisa Knapp Curtis, a journalist who is covering President Cleveland's forthcoming visit to New York. She won the Tony for her role in Kimberly Akimbo, and she also originated the role of Pamela in Head Over Heels.

Theater kids like me also likely clocked that Taylor Trensch recently made his debut on The Gilded Age as well. He's playing Oliver, the new bumbling footman for the van Rhijn household. I was first introduced to his work on stage in Bare: The Musical, but he's also been seen on Broadway in Dear Evan Hansen, Wicked, Hello, Dolly! and more. It seems like Oliver is going to be struggling with the new gig, although I'm going to be waiting for him to belt out some tunes in every scene.

With so many Broadway stars part of the massive Gilded Age cast, it feels like having a musical episode is a no-brainer. We've seen various shows have these types of specials before, including Buffy the Vampire Slayer, Scrubs, and Grey's Anatomy. None of those titles had the amount of accomplished musical theater performers that the HBO series has, so I'd imagine that The Gilded Age would blow people away if it allowed its cast to show off their vocal talents.

I'm not the only one who has been hoping to see a musical episode of The Gilded Age. While it remains to be seen if this happens, fans were treated to Voices of The Gilded Age: The Christmas Album, which features the cast of the show singing holiday tunes. That's the closest thing we've got to a musical episode for the time being, but maybe it'll help drum up excitement for that to happen in the future. Fingers crossed.

The Gilded Age airs new episodes Sundays on HBO As part of the 2026 TV schedule. We'll have to see if I ever get my wish of a full-blown musical episode, but for now I'll be streaming the Christmas album.

#3732. Switch 2 US sales soar again thanks to The Legend of Zelda effect, as it enjoys its best week of the year so far

Could a remade Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time be exciting enough to revitalise Switch 2 hardware sales? That was the big question. And early sales figures suggest the answer is yes, it can.

The Switch 2, which had been declining in hardware sales over the last few months, just had its highest (dollar) sales week of 2026 in the US so far following the game's release, according to Circana analyst Mat Piscatella on Bluesky.

The accompanying Legend of Zelda: 40th Anniversary Edition console in particular is responsible for a notable jump in Switch 2 hardware dollar sales. The themed, special edition console has been popular, with various retailers immediately running out of stock and a rise in scalping.

It's worth noting that The Legend of Zelda: 40th Anniversary Edition console, priced $520 / £430, does not include a copy of the game. Also, because the console was released 29th October, and the Ocarina of Time remake on 5th November, their sales results will come in separate monthly reports.

The Ocarina of Time launch also caused US hardware spending to jump by 81 percent during the week ending 31st October compared to the same period last year.

Christian Donlan awarded The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time a glitzy five stars in Eurogamer's review, writing: "This is Ocarina as it's always been, as timeless and intricate, but it also has a vibrancy and clarity that makes it feel like it was just created last Wednesday."

The fact this is the cheapest way of getting Intel's G3 is both a boon for Acer and an indictment of the memory crisis. If you've gotta buy soon, this offers perhaps the best price-to-performance ratio above $1,000.

PC Gamer's got your back Our experienced team dedicates many hours to every review, to really get to the heart of what matters most to you. Find out more about how we evaluate games and hardware.

Intel's G3 Extreme is a mighty impressive chip, and easily the headline feature of Acer's Predator Atlas 8. If you're looking to get the best handheld Panther Lake chip right now, Acer has swooped in at pretty much the cheapest price point on the market.

And if that's all you want, the Atlas 8 has my blessing. It's a solid device that makes use of the chip and offers compromises in memory and storage capacity (in the American market) to bring that cost down. Not only that, but if you buy one right now, you get a heaping of goodies with it.

But if you don't need top-of-the-line specs to have a good time, the Atlas 8 instead becomes just one of many very, very solid, yet very, very expensive handhelds on offer in a time that has become worse and worse thanks to the memory crisis.

✅ You want the G3 Extreme but cheaper: The Atlas 8 undercuts both MSI and OneXPlayer in pricing for a G3 Extreme handheld.

❌ You play fighters or platformers primarily: The D-pad is mushy and lacks distinction, making it unsatisfying and a tad unruly.

The fact this is the cheapest way of getting Intel's G3 is both a boon for Acer and an indictment of the memory crisis. If you've gotta buy soon, this offers perhaps the best price-to-performance ratio above $1,000.

8-inch WUXGA 1920 x 1200 (120 Hz refresh rate and 500 nits peak brightness)

The memory capacity is around average (Though lower than the high-end G3 Extreme offerings from MSI and OneXPlayer), and the storage is below average for a high-end handheld if you buy it in America.

Though 512 GB of storage isn't awful in a device you only want for gaming, the G3 Extreme is strong enough to take on even beefy, big-budget games, so it's a shame that the Atlas 8 can't hold all that many at once.

You are getting a strong feature set even outside of that chip, though. For one, TMR Sticks make for not only more efficient battery usage, but snappy, responsive controls. And you get Hall effect triggers too.

In a handful of games, with upscaling on and off (35 W plugged in)

Performance is the name of the game for the Acer Predator Atlas 8, and boy, does it perform. Compared to the Z2 Extreme, I saw figures generally between 30% and 50% better, but it manages to double the fps in Metro Exodus.

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

That performance bump is especially noticeable in games like Black Myth: Wukong, which are just below what I'd consider playable on Z2 Extreme and just about playable on the G3 Extreme. The G3 Extreme is the best gaming handheld chip right now, and the Atlas 8 getting less capacious memory than the MSI Claw 8 Ex AI+ CG3EM does not hold it back much in my testing. In fact, in some places, it even performs ever so slightly better.

Scores in major productivity suites and benchmarking tools (35 W plugged in)

At 860 grams, the Atlas 8 is a bit on the heavy side. It's balanced well, not feeling particularly heavy on either side, but you do notice that weight after long gaming sessions. I'm fond of the textured grips, but I do feel spoiled by the Asus ROG Xbox Ally X20 I used prior, thanks to its great feel and small cutaway between the screen and the grips.

However, I would simply pick a different handheld if you are planning on playing a heavy amount of fighting games or platformers, as the D-Pad is mushy, making it not only lacking in accuracy but generally unsatisfying to use. It's hard to make out when you actually hit buttons on the D-Pad, and it has very little distinction between different directions, making corner hits quite awkward. In Animal Well, I swapped to the thumbstick and never looked back.

The triggers and bumpers are solid, though, and the macro buttons on the back are satisfying to hit. You can even use a toggle just under the triggers to swap them from micro switches to full travel. That's an on-the-fly level of customisation that's admirable at best, and unnoticeable at worst.

Everything else about the Acer Predator Atlas 8 feels high quality in terms of feel. It's sturdy, with buttons placed well, and they're satisfyingly clacky without being too loud. The sound on the triggers is too hollow for my liking, but they feel smooth to the touch and are plenty responsive.

Speaking of loud, the speakers built into the Atlas 8 can really thump. They are in the bottom left and bottom right of the device, near the screen, making them quite immersive in use. They're not the highest quality, with the clashing of steel sounding more tinny than I'd usually ask for, but they're certainly not bad given their size.

With fans set to auto and performance mode at the 35 W Turbo mode, the fans are noticeable (once again, I have been spoiled by the X20), especially in intensive games like Phantom Blade Zero. But they're not so loud that they would put me off using this handheld in its high-wattage mode. I measured the fans to be around 40 decibels at their peak (around a whisper), with it averaging 28-35 decibels in intensive games. Whilst benchmarking, that went up to the 50-decibel mark, though only very briefly.

Acer says it has equipped the Atlas 8 with a custom Predator AeroBlade cooling, and in practice, it's certainly cooler than the likes of the Asus ROG Xbox Ally X and Lenovo Legion G S (though it doesn't beat the X20).

It certainly gets fairly hot internally, but with the fans pointing upwards, I never noticed any of that heat on my fingertips.

Recorded in HW Info whilst performing gaming benchmarks (35 W plugged in)

Windows on a handheld can still be awkward. The Atlas 8 comes built in with Xbox's handheld software, which is somewhat like Microsoft's attempt at Steam, but it's not totally smooth sailing in any direction (though it's more efficient than Windows). For instance, you can't get Intel drivers through the Acer Predator software built into the device as you might expect, so you still have to go through the Intel updater or search the internet, except with a touchscreen. And the Xbox mode still opens up Steam independently if you want to play a Steam game.

As well as this, the Atlas 8 has two dedicated buttons to open up Acer's software, the Acer Predator Sense, but it doesn't always work on the first try, and I haven't figured out exactly why this is yet. The button on the left-hand side opens up a quick bar-style version of the app to swap between performance modes, change resolution, etc. The button on the right-hand side opens the full-fat Predator Sense app, where you can get more granular with your customisation.

Though it's effectively the same setup as the Asus ROG Xbox Ally X, it's slower and more cumbersome. That seems to be the prevailing truth of pretty much any Windows-based handheld right now.

I notice next to no difference between the 25W Quiet Mode and 30W Balanced Mode, with mere minutes being between them in the PC Mark 10 battery life gaming test.

However, Panther Lake's battery-saving mode (thanks to what Intel calls Endurance Gaming) is truly great, providing just under three hours of battery life. For less intensive use cases, I could see much better battery life. This Endurance mode can be flicked between three different modes, with one end bringing down power for better battery life, and the other bringing that power up in exchange for less battery life. The middle Balanced Mode is how I would use the handheld day-to-day.

The only downside here is that the very lightest mode on the Atlas 8 is currently 25 W, which is the max on Z2 Extreme handhelds. You can push that down below 25 W, but you have to set a custom wattage, which I'd wager many handheld owners don't want to mess with. For most, you will be using this between 25 W and 35 W day-to-day.

Recorded using PCMark 10's gaming battery life test (Asus only goes up to 25 W unplugged but Acer goes up to 35 W)

Other than its fairly pretty face buttons, the Atlas 8 is a rather plain all-black gaming handheld. It goes without much intricate detailing (other than the Acer Predator RGB logo on the back and RGB rings around the thumbsticks).

As far as the display is concerned, you aren't getting any sort of fancy OLED here, but you do get a genuinely quite bright (500 nits) 16:10 WUXGA IPS display with Corning Gorilla Glass, making it decent in high-light environments. Importantly, I managed to play this out and about, and in front of a window, and could actually make out the game on screen, which is solid.

As of right now, it seems like the only model of the Atlas 8 with a G3 Extreme chip that sells in America comes with 512 GB of storage. That means you are getting half the storage and 75% of the memory of the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ CG3EM for 72% of the cost. But, as far as performance is concerned, I got pretty much identical stats, even beating out the Claw in 3DMark and losing in storage performance. That extra 8 GB of memory is unlikely to provide a major uplift in games, though the extra storage will certainly come in handy. My money would be on the Atlas 8 here.

Then, for the same price, one could pick up the Asus ROG Xbox Ally X20 (or the X for $300 less). Asus has the edge in ergonomics, look, thermals, screen, and storage capacity, but the G3 Extreme is a beast of a chip, handily handing Asus its butt in games. If you have got to pay upwards of $1,000 on a handheld right now, there's actually a good argument to be made for all three devices, though the Atlas 8 offers the best performance-to-price ratio.

It's a shame that Acer has to make little compromises to get that price down, but for $1,300, you will not get a better-performing gaming handheld in my book, and that's still quite impressive.

3. Best high performance: MSI Claw 8 EX AI+

#3730. Under pressure, Big Walk studio reveals it used generative AI "sparingly" while making its hit 2026 game

"It has become a matter of public interest."

Australian developer House House has revealed it used generative AI "sparingly" to help make celebrated, indie, multiplayer puzzle game Big Walk.

In a statement sent to Aftermath - following a judging fallout related to the Independent Games Festival - House House revealed it had used large language models primarily to help debug the game's code.

"In the final stretch of Big Walk's development, LLMs were used sparingly by House House to help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs," the developer said. "In some cases, snippets from LLM responses were copied as a starting point to be modified into game code - we'd estimate that well under 0.1 percent of Big Walk's code had anything to do with this usage, and generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game."

House House added: "The primary use case for House House's use of LLMs was to research, via chatbots, issues we encountered with third-party code."

The studio's revelation comes after a sizeable number of IGF jurors - 19 of them - issued a statement saying they would not vote for any game that used generative AI during its development. This was done after seeing "a significant increase" in entry submissions involving generative AI use, which "set off some fairly intense discussion and disagreement across the judge and jury pools". And rather than not vote for these in silence, a collection of jurors decided to take a public stand.

House House hadn't disclosed Big Walk generative AI use anywhere before disclosing it for its IGF submission. "We have not made any disclosure on Steam as the platform does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage," the studio explained. "We are posting this disclosure as it has become a matter of public interest."

House House added: "This is not an endorsement of, or argument for, the use of AI tools, however minimal. We have some concern that voluntary disclosures like this might contribute to the normalisation of this technology, or its treatment as 'inevitable'. We support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to video games and our world, and apologise that Big Walk's LLM usage may not meet their standards.

"Big Walk was developed without an internal AI usage policy in place, and we consider that lack of policy a failure. We will work to have a more comprehensive policy going forwards."

It's a revelation that's likely to leave a taint of some degree on one of this year's brightest stars - a game Eurogamer awarded a full five stars to in its Big Walk review.

#3729. Report: James Gunn Ousted Amid Messy Power Struggle Despite Superman’s Success

ClayfaceDC StudiosJames GunnPeter SafranSupergirlSuperman

Yesterday, James Gunn and Peter Safran stepped down from their positions as co-presidents at DC Studios. This was after just four years on the job and only three movies in the new superhero cinematic universe they were overseeing. The pair has now been replaced by ex-Marvel producer Jeremy Latcham, whose evangelical history has given some DC fans pause. So what happened? According to a new report by The Hollywood Reporter, trouble had been brewing for the pair as soon as the Skydance merger went through earlier this year.

According to THR‘s sources, on Friday, November 6, Skydance co-CEOs David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz informed the pair that, despite previously being told they would be part of the company moving forward, there had been a “change of plans.” The shake-up had reportedly been in the works since “early fall,” with Latcham having been contacted about potentially taking over DC Studios by Skydance Motion Picture Group co-chair John Greenstein, who worked with Latcham during his time at Marvel.

THR says that there were multiple points of “tension” between Gunn and Safran on one hand and the Skydance execs on the other. Gunn and Safran initially reported directly to Warner Bros. CEO David Zaslav, and their contracts said they would maintain that kind of direct reporting structure even in the event of a change in leadership, so they would have reported to Ellison following the merger. Meanwhile, Greenstein and co-chair Dana Goldberg were reportedly trying to consolidate movie production under their leadership, while Gunn and Safran had grown “accustomed to having strong control” over anything under the DC Studios banner.

Other points of contention included that Gunn and Safran were reportedly âslowâ and “not forthcoming” in sharing plans and footage with the Skydance leads.

Many will point to Supergirl‘s box office bomb as a sticking point, and I’ve even seen a lot of people joke that Gunn and Safran only got “one bad movie” before they were thrown out. While Supergirl‘s performance is noted as a problem by THR‘s sources, apparently even their biggest hit, Superman, wasn’t doing enough in the eyes of their corporate overlords. That film, which grossed $618 million on a $225 budget, “did not net out, or have the kind of pop culture impact, in the way that kind of movie should,” in the eyes of Skydance.

Sources say that Gunn is “somewhat relieved” to be out of the business side of things and now focusing on filmmaking. His DC next film, Man of Tomorrow, is set to premiere next year.

As for Latcham, THR‘s sources call him a “down-the-middle shooter” who is more concerned with making “hits for the masses” than Gunn, whose projects often feature somewhat profane writing and obscure characters.

Clayface, the last DC Studios project produced while Gunn and Safran were company co-presidents, is in theaters now.
